The Sarkylmas Kuat Wind Power Project is a greenfield Independent Power Project located in the Mangystau Region of Kazakhstan. The Project involves the construction and operation of a 50 MW wind farm to provide renewable energy to Kazakhstan’s national electricity grid(KEGOC).

The project involves the deployment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) to store electricity generated from renewable energy sources such as solar or wind. The BESS enables time-shifting of renewable energy by storing surplus electricity during periods of low demand and discharging it during peak demand periods or grid stress events. This reduces the need for fossil fuel-based peaking power plants and supports grid stability and renewable energy integration. The system comprises battery, power conversion systems (inverters), battery management systems, and control software to optimize charging/discharging cycles. The project contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions by displacing grid electricity that would otherwise be generated from fossil fuels.

Promoting Regenerative Agriculture for Nature (PRAN)” is a Programme of Activities (PoA) to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from rice farming based on traditional practices like continuous flooding in India. The PoA will implement improved water management techniques, such as intermittent flooding, alternate wetting and drying (AWD), direct seeded rice (DSR) and regenerative farming practices etc. in rice paddies across India. The PoA applies the Gold Standard Methodology for methane emission Reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation, version 1.0.

The proposed Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) is developed by Grow Indigo Private Limited and is implemented across states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh in India. VPA implements improved water management techniques, such as intermittent flooding, alternate wetting and drying (AWD), direct seeded rice (DSR) and regenerative farming practices, etc. in rice paddies. This initiative aims to introduce and promote improved agricultural techniques specifically for rice farming, falling under the Land Use & Forestry (LUF) and Agriculture (AGR) categories.

The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Uganda project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the Western (Afromontane) highlands and pastoral rangelands of mid-Western Uganda. Over several decades, these regions have experienced substantial deforestation and degradation, poor agriculture practices, overgrazing, and an unsustainable demand for fuelwood. Climate change, population increases, poverty and lack of economic opportunities further exacerbate pressure on the land. The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in 24 districts in Western Uganda involving more than 200,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services. The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.

The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Malawi project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the in the Northern, Central and Southern Regions of the country. Over 90% of households in the country depend on natural resources and subsistence agriculture to meet their livelihoods, food and energy needs. Extensive clearing of forest and woodlands for fuelwood, followed by conversion to cropland, is driving a high annual deforestation rate of 1%. The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in seven districts in Malawi involving more than 150,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services. The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.

The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Coastal Kenya project is implemented in Kenya’s coastal region, specifically in the Kwale and Kilifi counties. With an annual deforestation rate of 0.58%, Kenya faces significant forest loss, primarily driven by dependence on natural resources and extensive land degradation. The primary causes of land degradation include unsustainable wood resource exploitation, the expansion of unsustainable cultivation practices, the spread of invasive species, pollution, and climate change. The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in the Kwale and Kilifi counties in Kenya, involving more than 100,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include increased household income, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services. The project builds on extensive experience in socio-economic development within the region.

The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Kenya and Rift Valley Kenya project is implemented in Kenya’s Elgeyo-Marakwet, Migori and Narok counties. Over several decades, these counties have experienced substantial deforestation and degradation because of poor agricultural practices, overgrazing and unsustainable demand for fuelwood. The scenario - the continued degradation of land and erosion of livelihood opportunities – will most likely continue to occur unless there is a substantial and additional intervention The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in the Elgeyo-Marakwet, Migori and Narok counties in Kenya, involving more than 75,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include increased household income, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.

The regular case voluntary project activity (VPA) is providing household water filtration units for marginalized households in India living in rural, urban, semi-urban areas. The VPA is a part of POA and its real case VPA, which will contribute to the reduction of greenhouse gases and socio-economic progress for communities who are relying on unsafe drinking water sources and thus the objective of the VPA is to disseminate household water treatment units in Madhya Pradesh, India so that the rural communities living in remote hilly areas have increased access of safe drinking water for their daily use and thus increased living standard for the poor and marginalized people. The regular case VPA under the GS Programme of Activity provides safe household drinking water treatment solutions to marginalized households at free of cost and replace the usage of equivalent quantity of fuel wood in traditional three stone fire or any other conventional wood stoves which are inefficient and smoke-intensive and which would have been used to boil the water to make it safe for drinking purposes.

The project aims to bring a positive impact in the livelihoods of project beneficiaries by disseminating improved cooking devices in Nepal. The project ICSs will replace traditional/inefficient biomass stoves currently used as baseline technologies. The prevalent use of such traditional cooking systems in Nepal results in significant greenhouse gas emissions from the use of non-renewable biomass (NRB), which is often sourced unsustainably. Additionally, traditional biomass-based cooking generates high levels of smoke and particulate matter (PM), exposing the primary cook—usually women—to hazardous indoor air pollution (IAP). The improved cookstoves (ICSs) introduced by the project are designed to be thermally more efficient, reducing fuel consumption, cooking time, and emissions. As a result, the project contributes to GHG emission reductions while also creating a cleaner cooking environment and reducing IAP exposure for women and children.

The "Idea Balance Safe Water Access Project" will be implemented on Zanzibar Island, part of the United Republic of Tanzania. The project focuses on rehabilitating non-functional boreholes that have not received maintenance from the government or any authorized entity. These efforts will be financed and coordinated by the IDEA Universal International Development and Environment Association (IDEA Universal), leveraging their extensive expertise in sustainable water access initiatives. This initiative aims to restore orphaned boreholes, identified based on household need and proximity to communities without alternative drinking water sources within a 1 km radius. By providing access to safe and clean drinking water, the project intends to reduce greenhouse gas emissions associated with boiling unsafe water and to decrease reliance on non-renewable biomass, mitigating environmental degradation and promoting sustainable resource use.

The purpose of the VPA is to disseminate Safe Water Supply (SWS) devices such as Institutional water treatment (IWT) and Household Water Treatment (HWT) technologies and Improved cookstoves in households and communities of Rwanda, Africa. The filters and/or Improved cookstoves are distributed to households/institutions which were earlier using wood and/or charcoal on rudimentary stoves for cooking/boiling or were consuming untreated water, for households where filters are distributed. The project makes the end-users energy efficient and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions otherwise resulting from the burning of non-renewable woody biomass and/or charcoal in baseline scenario. The project boundary is the geographical boundary of Rwanda, Africa where the water filters/Improved cookstoves are proposed to be distributed.

The purpose of this Real VPA is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in industry in Kenya by reducing the use of energy from heavy fuel oil in the baseline by substituting it with renewable biomass briquettes, made from bagasse which is a waste stream from the sugar industry. Sugar is an annual crop and therefore renewable . The fuel oil in the baseline is deemed “non-renewable”. The main greenhouse gas being reduced by the project is carbon dioxide. More specifically, Tamuwa Limited (the Project Implementer) sells briquettes to Kensalt in Malindi that makes edible salt from sea water.

Infosys Limited the project developer along with implementation partners is implementing Agroforestry projects in India. The project aims to enhance the livelihood of farmers and local communities. The primary aim of the project is to improve the social, economic and environmental conditions of the community along with estimating the carbon sequestration capacity thorough agroforestry in alignment with the SDG goals.

The purpose of the project is to generate electricity by harnessing the solar and wind energy by using solar photovoltaic & Wind turbine generator technologies and there by feed the generated electricity to the Indian national grid. Project involves the installation of 60 MW Solar Photovoltaic Power Plant & Wind power plant combined with BESS (60 MWh) in Uruchinthala, Tadipatri Tehsil, Dist. Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh. The project is yet to be commissioned and the generated electricity will be continuously supplied to the Indian grid. The power purchase agreement had been signed for the project on 31/07/2024 between SOLAR ENERGY CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED and CLEAN RENEWABLE ENERGY BARMER PRIVATE LIMITED. with rated capacity of renewable energy components as: Solar – 75 MWac; Wind Power – 79.2 MW; and ESS – 60/60 MW/60 MWh.

The Programme of Activities (PoA) “TASC SOLUM - Sequestration and Optimised Landscapes Using Microbials” aims to improve the health of agricultural land in South Africa by using natural biostimulants to enhance soil carbon sequestration. The main goal of the project is to remove carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and store it permanently in agricultural soils, which is good for the environment and can help reduce the effects of climate change by decreasing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG). Current intensive and high-input forms of agriculture are leading to biodiversity loss, soil erosion, poor water retention, decreased drought resilience, GHG emissions, decreased plant health and nutrition, and decreased soil health. Applying regenerative agricultural practices addresses these issues via several ways, including precision application of biological and chemical inputs, minimising soil disturbance, inter-cropping, cover cropping, and integrating livestock when possible. This project within the regenerative agriculture programme will focus on the precision application of biological and chemical inputs. More specifically, the application of biostimulants for soil revitalisation.

Mozambique is classified as a Least Developed Country by the United Nations, and only half of Mozambicans have access to improved water supply in rural areas. Handpumps, which are commonly found in communities, often fall into disrepair shortly after installation due to insufficient maintenance, lack of access to spare parts, and financial support. The Pungue project, developed by Removall, aims to rehabilitate and sustain handpumps across Sofala province of Mozambique. It will avoid the consumption of firewood by households and lead to a reduction of carbon dioxide emissions.

The project will disseminate improved cook stoves (ICS) – to households within Tanzania. By providing clean cooking, the project will ensure that households consume less firewood during the process of cooking and as a result there shall be a reduction of carbon dioxide emissions from the combustion process. Most people in Sub-Saharan Africa rely on gathering biomass for cooking, in particular in rural areas, which dramatically damages health and impairs productivity improvements. The procurement and consumption of these fuels define the character of everyday life in many developing countries. In line to its vision of delivering high impact related to health, savings and convenience, SDG 13 Ventures Pte. Ltd. is undertaking an extensive distribution programme to create a nation-wide access of Clean Cookstoves for low-income consumer. The project will contribute in achieving SDGs including, SDG-01: 1 No poverty, SDG-3: Good Health and Well Being, SDG-5: Gender Equality, SDG 7- Affordable and Clean energy, SDG 8: Full and productive employment and decent work for all, SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities and SDG-13: Climate Action. The programme would result in GHG emission reductions and other impact outcomes which can be traded internationally and the revenue collected from such trade will benefit the scaling up of the project and thereby assist other households who are still using traditional stoves.

This project seeks to reduce carbon emissions by providing new clean water sources to rural villages in Uganda where the only means of access to clean water is to collect it from surface ponds and streams and boiling it for safe use. This real case is for a set of 10 villages in the Bunyoro-Kitara area of Western Uganda that will be provided with a new borehole for actual GHG emission reduction through the provision of clean water.

The ATEC Biodigesters in Bangladesh project is designed to serve rural households that primarily rely on fi rewood and biomass fuels for cooking. The primary target group consists of small-scale farming households that own 3 to 5 cows, as they can eff ectively utilize biogas technology to meet their cooking needs. This initiative aims to tackle the pressing challenges of clean cooking, environmental degradation, and rural household energy dependence by providing sustainable cooking solutions for low-income households. By introducing ATEC’s biodigesters and biogas stoves, this project will replace traditional firewood stoves with highly efficient and eco-friendly alternatives. Beyond environmental benefits, the project is designed to improve the well-being of household members, particularly women, infants, and children. By reducing exposure to indoor air pollution, it helps lower the risk of respiratory illnesses and related health expenses. Additionally, it alleviates the burden of fi rewood collection, freeing up valuable time for education, economic activities, and improved quality of life.

The Sun Power Project is a 30 MW (AC) photovoltaic solar plant located in the municipality of Nagarote, within the department of León, Nicaragua. This facility will comprise 62,070 solar modules, achieving a total installed capacity of 38 MWp and a net capacity of 30 MW. The primary objective of this project is to contribute to the development of Nicaragua's electricity sector while adhering to sustainability principles and fostering the transformation of the country's energy matrix towards renewable and clean energy sources. The solar park aims to comply with international climate change mitigation standards, aligning with worldwide efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote a more sustainable future. In conclusion, the SunPower Project is not only designed to enhance Nicaragua’s energy supply but also plays a pivotal role in supporting the country's commitments to environmental sustainability and facilitating the transition to a cleaner, more responsible energy matrix.

1. Project Design and Scenarios The project aims to collect and treat landfill gas (Landfill Gas – LFG) in various scenarios to reduce methane emissions. The planned scenarios include: •Controlled flaring of collected gas; •Supplying treated gas to industrial, commercial, or residential consumers; •Using gas as fuel for electricity generation. These scenarios will be applied according to the specific characteristics and needs of each landfill included in the program. At the Santa Rosa Waste Treatment Center (CTR) in Seropédica (Rio de Janeiro – Brazil), the current scenario involves the capture of landfill gas (LFG) for combustion and distribution to external consumers. In the future, infrastructure is planned for electricity generation from the collected gas. 2. Technologies and Measures The project uses modern technologies for LFG capture, treatment, and utilization, such as: •Vertical and horizontal wells for gas collection; •High-efficiency flaring systems; •Infrastructure for gas treatment, including contaminant removal; •Infrastructure for transporting biogas by trucks for external thermal applications. For future phases, CTR Santa Rosa also plans to install modular equipment for electricity generation. Additionally, the project includes strict monitoring to ensure operational efficiency and safety. 3. Geographic Boundaries Currently, the project only includes CTR Santa Rosa in Seropédica/RJ. Geographic coordinates: -22.795703 (latitude) and -43.760558 (longitude).

The Indonesia Sustainable Ride Program by EcoSecurities (PoA) aims to distribute electric or hybrid vehicles in Indonesia. The distribution and usage of electric or hybrid vehicles will reduce the consumption of gasoline and other fossil fuel from the use of regular fuel-combustion engine vehicles. This reduced consumption will reduce the amount of greenhouse gas emission resulting from the vehicles usage.

The Sustainable Electric Motorbike Ride Project by ESB and EcoSecurities (VPA) aims to promote the adoption of electric motorbikes by making them more accessible through the sales or rental of up to 501,000 electrics motor bikes or scooters over 5 to 6 year time in Indonesia as part of the PoA. The use of electric motor bikes and scooters to replace conventional fuel-powered motorbikes will reduce the consumption of gasoline and other fossil fuels consumed in regular fuel-combustion motorcycle. With the reduced consumption, the amount of greenhouse gas emission resulting from the motorcycle usage will also decrease, contributing to a more sustainable transportation system.

Erguvan Enerji Elektrik Üretim A.Ş. plans to launch the Göktepe Wind Power Plant Capacity Increase Project with a total installed capacity of 105.64 MWm / 105.64 MWe, based on the Electricity Generation License obtained from the Energy Market Regulatory Authority on 04/06/2020. The project will be implemented within the borders of Esenköy in Çınarcık District, and Mecidiye Village and Karşıyaka in Armutlu District, Yalova Province. As part of the project, 19 wind turbines will be constructed and a Battery Energy Storage System will also be established. The electricity generated at the plant will be transmitted to the Yalova WPP and Yares Yalova WPP Transformer Substations via a 154 kV transmission line. Scheduled to be commissioned in 2029, the Göktepe Wind Power Plant Capacity Increase Project is expected to supply approximately 260,625 MWh of electricity annually to the grid. Due to its renewable energy source, the wind power plant will also contribute to a reduction of approximately 165,366 tons of CO₂ equivalent emissions per year.

This project aims to reduce the reliance on non-renewable biomass for cooking by introducing efficient, clean cooking technologies across Nigeria. This goal will be achieved through the distribution and installation of the EcoHome stoves.
Installation of solar water supply systems with community tap stands and hand pumps across Plateau State, Northern Nigeria

Voluntary Project Activity 2 (VPA-2) under the HECTOR project represents a transformative initiative aimed at rural villages in the Anantapur District of Andhra Pradesh. This project is specifically designed to tackle the critical issues surrounding the availability of safe drinking water, aligning with the broader goals of India's Jal Jivan Mission. VPA-2 focuses on revolutionizing water purification by introducing advanced technologies, including automated chlorination units, UV disinfection systems, and real-time water quality monitoring powered by IoT and AI-ML. The strategic implementation of these solutions seeks to address the persistent challenges in rural areas, significantly improving water quality standards and enhancing access to safe drinking water for the communities involved.

The “Resilient Futures” Programme of Activities (PoA) is a community-driven initiative designed to address the interlinked challenges of poverty, environmental degradation, and climate change across vulnerable rural regions. By deploying scalable, high-impact interventions—such as improved cookstoves, safe water technologies, biochar production, and regenerative agroforestry—this PoA aims to reduce and remove greenhouse gas emissions while strengthening the adaptive capacity of local communities. Led by trusted local partners and supported by ethical climate finance, the PoA empowers women, improves health outcomes, restores ecosystems, and increases household income and food security. This programme contributes to multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land). The PoA is designed to enable the rapid scaling of ethical, verifiable carbon projects in West Africa and beyond—delivering measurable climate impact and real, lasting change for people and planet.

The Empowering Communities Through Improved Cookstoves project in rural Togo distributes fuel-efficient improved cookstoves (ICS) to replace traditional, inefficient three-stone fires commonly used in rural households. The cookstoves are manufactured locally in Togo, supporting infrastructure development, generating employment, and stimulating economic growth in the region. By reducing the amount of firewood required for cooking, the project alleviates the time and physical burden of firewood collection—a task that disproportionately falls on women and girls. This, in turn, enables greater access to education and income-generating opportunities. In addition to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, the project delivers a range of co-benefits, including: Improved indoor air quality, reducing the incidence of respiratory and eye-related illnesses caused by smoke inhalation from traditional stoves. Reduced pressure on local forests through decreased firewood demand, slowing deforestation and preserving biodiversity. Lower household expenditure on cooking fuel due to more efficient wood use. Increased time savings for women and children, enabling greater focus on education, caregiving, and economic activities. Job creation and skill development through local cookstove production and distribution. By addressing both climate change and local development needs, the project contributes to eight Sustainable Development Goals.

The Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project is a scalable initiative focused on restoring the historically mangrove-rich wetlands of the Niger Delta through a community-led approach. The Niger Delta—the largest river delta in Africa and home to the world’s third-largest mangrove forest—has faced severe degradation over the past decades due to a variety of pressures. This has compromised biodiversity, diminished livelihoods, and increased vulnerability to flooding and erosion for the 30 million people who live there. This project aims to restore the ecosystem through training local communities to plant native, locally adapted mangrove species, while also addressing the causes of mangrove loss. Its objectives are to: • Empower communities by providing the livelihood support, education, and tools needed to become long-term ecosystem stewards and bolster their resilience in a climate-changing world, • Restore a critical ecosystem and its services while promoting biodiversity by rebuilding the habitats of numerous species, strengthening regional food security, and providing flood and storm protection. • And finally, sequester carbon in the fight against climate change while utilizing mangroves as a powerful nature-based solution. Rooted in strong local partnerships and ecosystem restoration approaches, the project is designed to scale and serve as a model for community-first restoration across Nigeria and the wider region.

UpEnergy Group will work with micro-entrepreneurs, NGOs, financial institutions, local distribution partners etc. to provide residential/institutions users with clean cooking technologies. UpEnergy would ensure the last-mile distribution/installation of the energy efficient/clean energy technologies to the beneficiaries. This VPA is implemented in host country-Zambia.

The VPA aims to positively impact the livelihoods of farmers in Bangladesh by promoting the adoption of the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method in rice cultivation. This improved farming practice replaces the traditional continuous flooding technique, which contributes to significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions due to methane release from waterlogged fields. The AWD method optimizes water usage by alternating periods of wetting and drying, which not only reduces water consumption but also enhances soil aeration, improving nutrient uptake. As a result, the activity substantially reduces methane emissions, leading to lower overall GHG emissions. By introducing AWD practice, the activity supports sustainable water management and environmental sustainability in the region. Bangladesh Bondhu Foundation is the Project Developer as well as the VPA Implementer for this Program of Activity. Climate Secure serves as the CME.

The AWD method optimizes water usage by alternating periods of wetting and drying, which not only reduces water consumption but also enhances soil aeration, improving nutrient uptake. As a result, the activity substantially reduces methane emissions, leading to lower overall GHG emissions. By introducing AWD practice, the activity supports sustainable water management and environmental sustainability in the region. Bangladesh Bondhu Foundation is the Project Developer as well as the VPA Implementer for this Program of Activity. Climate Secure serves as the CME.

The project aims to restore and maintain non-functional boreholes in rural, water-scarce regions of South Africa. By providing reliable access to clean groundwater, it reduces dependence on unsafe water sources and the need to boil water using traditional fuels. The initiative also builds local capacity by training and employing community technicians for ongoing maintenance, ensuring long-term sustainability and resilience. The project improves access to safe drinking water, leading to a reduction in waterborne diseases and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the use of traditional fuels for water purification. It lessens the burden on women and children by minimizing the time spent collecting water, enhances community health and safety, creates local employment opportunities, and promotes awareness of safe water and hygiene practices.

The proposed project is a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) focused on afforestation and will be implemented in Odisha, India. It aims to sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide through plantations. The project will promote native and climate-resilient species, with the special emphasis to support sustainable livelihoods through community participation and agroforestry practices. It will also enhance biodiversity and improve soil health. Furthermore, the project generates temporary employment for local communities during the implementation and management of the plantation. The project aligns with multiple SDGs, including climate action, life on land, and no poverty.

Project Saladillo transforms 15,946 hectares of cattle grazing land, subject to continual slash-and-burn practices, in Paraguay’s Cordillera region into a mosaic plantation combining commercial and conservation forestry. It prioritises long-term ecological resilience and sustainable development. The project integrates 25% permanent conservation with 75% selectively harvested forestry, maintaining at least 96% continuous forest cover. This model prevents deforestation by producing sustainable timber and biomass, while enhancing biodiversity through protection of native forests and riparian corridors, supporting habitat continuity and safeguarding local fauna. An estimated 1,122,437 tons of CO₂ will be sequestered over 50+ years. High-precision carbon monitoring uses LiDAR-based models calibrated with field sampling to ensure accuracy in both accessible and remote areas. Saladillo generates formal, year-round employment through staggered planting and harvesting, eliminating informal labour, reducing seasonal risks, and ensuring steady income for local communities. It collaborates closely with local NGOs such as Fundación Moisés Bertoni and the University of Asunción, integrating community engagement, biodiversity monitoring, and academic research. The project adheres to the highest environmental and social safeguards, aligning with FSC certification, IFC Performance Standards, and World Bank guidelines, contributing to SDGs 8, 12, 13, and 15.

The project aims to promote agroforestry practices by planting coconut trees (Cocos nucifera) on fallow farmland systems in the Indian state of Karnataka. This coconut plantation initiative falls under the Afforestation and Reforestation (A/R) project activity, focusing on implementing agroforestry practices to enhance the resilience, productivity, and sustainability of farming systems by enhancing farmer income. The project developer Sow & Reap Agro Pvt. Ltd. aims to achieve the goals of (a) enhancing farmer income through climate resilient systems, and (b) mitigate the impact of climate change by sequestering atmospheric CO2 into coconut tree biomass.

The Madad Electric Cookstove (MEC) Project is abased clean energy initiative developed by Third Pole Solutions in partnership with the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme (AKRSP) as the coordinating and implementing agency in Pakistan. The project aims to replace traditional wood-burning stoves—locally known as bukhari—and 3-stone cooking methods with energy-efficient electric cookstoves. The Primary objectives of the Project is to reduce the use of wood for cooking, thereby reducing the GHG emissions and having a positive impact on the Climate (SDG 13). By adopting clean, sustainable cooking practices (SDG7), the Project will focus on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all by addressing the impact of environment factors on health (SDG3), reduce time spent on collecting or buying firewood resulting in cost savings and increasing the household's disposable income (SDG1) and promote gender equality by involving women's community groups (SDG5)

In most of the countries on the African continent including Ghana, cooking is done on either 3-stone fires or very inefficient traditional cookstoves, consuming a lot of fuel, in particular non-renewable firewood and charcoal. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils’ reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer. The purpose of a ‘STERLING IMPROVED COOKSTOVES PROJECT Carbon Project Activities included under the Gold Standard’, is to disseminate highly efficient improved cookstoves (ICS to urban, peri-urban and/or rural users (households, communities, institutions, or SMEs) in Ghana. Several greenhouse gases (GHG), including carbon dioxide, are produced as a result of the incomplete combustion of biomass as used in cook stoves. More GHG emissions result from the use of biomass which is non-renewable. ICS improves heat transfer efficiency as compared to the baseline traditional cook stoves, thereby reducing both the amount of woody biomass used by unit appliances implemented and the emission of GHGs.

The Ghana Cocoa Agroforestry Livelihoods Project is designed to enhance the productivity and long-term sustainability of cocoa farming systems while improving the livelihoods of the communities that depend on them. By introducing an agroforestry model that integrates shade tree species into existing cocoa plantations, the project aims to extend the productive lifespan of cocoa trees and strengthen the system’s resilience to environmental challenges, including pests and diseases. This initiative will be carried out in close partnership with the local communities, with a focus on engaging youth teams to lead on the ground implementation. The project is expected to reach 11,000 farmers for an implementation area of 17,000 hectares. The project’s main activity consists of planting shade and fruit trees within the existing cocoa plantations. Nine different native tree species will be incorporated into the farms to achieve a target density of 90 shade trees per hectare. Additionally, the new tree plantations will be associated with the training and coaching of the farmers in sustainable agroforestry practices such as tree management, pruning and Integrated Pest Management (IPM). The implementation of these practices is expected to increase the productive lifetime of the cocoa species and reduce the incidence of pests and diseases on the targeted trees. The project is expected to sequester 2.61 MtCO2e within 30 years.

The Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG) Programme of Activities (PoA) “The Cameroon Clean Households´ Energy Program” (the CCHEP PoA) aims at the introduction and distribution of innovative clean energy solutions to households in Cameroon. The PoA serves as a framework under which different Voluntary Project Activities (subprojects or “VPAs”) will be implemented.

The Heat Retention Cooking VPA No. 1 aims at distributing around 15,000 to 20,000 heat retention cooking bags, so called “Wonderbags”. These Wonderbags retain a large portion of cooking energy by storing dishes that are brought to the boiling point in a heat insulated bag, where the cooking process is finished without the need of further heating. Therefore, they greatly reduce the consumption of traditional cooking fuels, mainly fuelwood, charcoal and liquified petroleum gas (LPG).

The Carbono Vivo Marañón Project is a long-term environmental and climate initiative that supports the transition to sustainable land use through the establishment of agroforestry systems based on cashew (Anacardium occidentale) in Colombia. Designed to generate social, environmental, and climate benefits, the PoA brings together producers, processors, marketers, and local communities across the value chain to promote rural development, biodiversity conservation, and carbon removal.

Carbono Vivo Marañón KardiaNuts & Kashú is the first real-case VPA under the PoA, implemented in the department of Vichada, Colombia. It operationalizes the PoA framework by establishing the first set of agroforestry systems with cashew in collaboration with local stakeholders. The VPA focuses on generating measurable climate impact through carbon sequestration, while contributing to local livelihoods and sustainable land management.

The purpose of the Improved Cooking Project in Madagascar is to mitigate climate change by reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through the distribution of efficient cookstoves. This project aims to enhance environmental sustainability and improve the health and socio-economic conditions of rural and urban communities in Madagascar. By replacing traditional open-fire cooking methods with improved cookstoves, the project will significantly reduce fuel consumption, thereby decreasing deforestation rates and promoting the sustainable management of natural resources. The project aligns with the Gold Standard's objectives of delivering real, measurable, and long-term emission reductions and promoting sustainable development benefits.

The proposed project activity ‘Accelerating Access to Clean Cooking in Kenya Project by Nyalore Impact Limited’ will be implemented by Nyalore Impact Limited’ with the purpose of promoting and distributing clean cooking devices that include Induction Cookers (ICs) and Electric Pressure Cookers (EPCs) to house-holds in Kenya. The project intends to accelerate access to clean cooking by displacing use of inefficient biomass cooking devices and polluting fuels. Use of the project technology will displace GHG emissions from the thermal energy consumption required for cooking by households. This will consequently contribute towards reduced household air pollution and support several sustainable development goals. The project’s primary target is end-users who cook using inefficient biomass cookstoves and polluting fuels such as kerosene both in the urban and rural areas of Kenya. Goals and Objectives of the Project Activity According to the 2022 KNBS Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) report, 68.5% of Kenyan population still highly dependent on traditional cooking fuels, with firewood being the predominant cooking fuel. This presents a climate change challenge and has motivated the project developer to develop an innovative project that will accelerate the transition to cleaner cooking solutions to mitigate the negative impacts associated with the use of traditional fuels.

Infosys Limited is spearheading a visionary large-scale agroforestry initiative under a proposed Programme of Activities (PoA), spanning diverse regions across India. This transformative project focuses on restoring degraded lands through the plantation of a wide variety of climate-resilient agroforestry species. At its heart lies the active participation of local farmers and communities-empowering them through sustainable land-use practices that not only regenerate ecosystems but also enhance livelihoods. By blending traditional knowledge with modern ecological approaches, the project is committed to building climate resilience, enriching biodiversity, and fostering long-term socio-economic growth for rural communities.

The proposed initiative is a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) focused on agroforestry plantations, to be implemented in Odisha, India. Implemented by the SGI Foundation, the project aims to sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide through large-scale plantation activities, while simultaneously enhancing local biodiversity, improving soil health, and promoting sustainable livelihoods. The project emphasizes the cultivation of native and climate-resilient agroforestry species such as Mango, Teak, Cashew, Jackfruit, Guava, and other regionally suitable trees under the first VPA. Active participation from local farmers is central to the initiative, empowering them to adopt agroforestry practices that improve income security and resilience to climate variability. Beyond its environmental benefits, the project contributes significantly to socio-economic development by generating temporary employment for community members during the plantation's establishment and maintenance phases. It also strengthens long-term sustainability through capacity-building and inclusive community engagement. The initiative supports multiple SDGs, including Climate Action (SDG 13), Life on Land (SDG 15), and No Poverty (SDG 1), by integrating carbon sequestration with biodiversity conservation and rural development. A core objective of the project is to quantify the carbon sequestration potential of agroforestry plantations in Odisha while uplifting farming communities through sustainable land-use practices.

ATH Bioenergy is promoting the implementation of four organic waste recovery plants in the Canary Islands with the aim of transforming the waste generated in the hotel, commercial and agri-food sectors into biomethane and high-quality organic fertilisers with the use of CO2. This initiative represents a firm step towards the energy transition, the decarbonization of the territory, the promotion of a real circular economy in the archipelago, and the contribution to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals to which the Company is committed, positively impacting the local community.

The plant, located in the municipality of Agüimes, in Gran Canaria, is expected to come into operation in October 2025, at which time a three-month operational test phase will be carried out to guarantee the efficiency and safety of the process. The implementation to obtain emission reductions is estimated in the first quarter of 2026. This first plant will be located next to the Southeast treatment plant, in the port free zone of Gran Canaria, which will facilitate its logistical integration and connectivity with distribution channels. It will be designed to manage up to 31,000 tonnes of organic waste per year, from which approximately 2,242 tonnes of biomethane per year will be produced, equivalent to 31,141 MWh of energy. This production of this energy vector represents a sustainable alternative to about 2,832 tons of propane gas, which will allow a significant reduction in the use of fossil fuels and polluting gas emissions and contribute to local climate and energy governance. As for the size and scope of the activity of the facility, it is estimated that it can serve some 45-65 hotels since the capacity of the digester, is 31,000 t/y of organic waste. Among the key components of the project, the production of biomethane as a renewable substitute for propane gas and diesel stands out.

The Biomass Gasification VPA No. 1 aims at distributing biomass gasification cookstoves. These stoves, that allow for clean cooking with pellets and other biomass, will replace traditional cooking, mainly fuelwood and charcoal responsible for deforestation and indoor air pollution in Cameroon.

The main purpose of the project activity is the distribution of fuel-efficient improved cook stoves (ICS) specifically in the states of Nigeria. The Improved cook-stoves distributed through this project has replaced the low-efficient traditional cook-stoves. Through this project, the distribution and installation of high thermal efficient improved cook stoves (ICS) has been undertaken for households. The ICS burns non-renewable woody biomass and/or charcoal more efficiently thereby improving thermal energy transfer to pots, hence saving fuel wood and greenhouse gases. Not only will this halt the rapidly progressing deforestation but will also reduce health hazards from indoor air (smoke) pollution and women and children will have to spend less time collecting firewood.

This project introduces the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method in rice cultivation across the different districts of Eastern region of India. By adopting this water-saving irrigation technique, the project aims to significantly reduce methane emissions and optimize water usage, contributing to climate change mitigation and resource conservation. Beyond environmental benefits, the initiative seeks to empower local farmers through targeted training and capacity-building programs. The project also delivers tangible socio-economic co-benefits to farming communities, such as improved resilience, knowledge transfer, and potential income enhancement, thereby supporting sustainable rural development in the region.

This PoA aims to save water and reduce methane emissions during rice farming by introducing water management technology to rice farming, which is one of the main greenhouse gas emission sources in Cambodia. By participating in this project, farmers can produce low-carbon rice without reducing rice productivity and participate in mitigating climate change. ThanksCarbon, a business developer, has introduced an AI-based satellite technology into this project to reduce the burden on individual farmers for data collection and improve the convenience of monitoring data collection and MRV transparency. Farmers will be motivated and trained to refrain from continuously flooding their fields by putting the suggested AWD technology into effect, which would cut down on the quantity of CH4 emissions that would have been produced in the baseline situation. The sole change made to the project scenario is the adoption of alternating wetting and drying conditions rather than the submerged condition. Other than that, the project keeps the current agricultural techniques in place and does not introduce any new activities that might increase greenhouse gas emissions.

The “Avoiding Methane Emissions through Composting at DN Agrar, Romania” project aims to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions by implementing controlled aerobic composting of raw dairy manure at two farms located in Alba and Hunedoara counties. Traditionally, manure is managed through open stockpiling or storage in lagoons, practices that lead to uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition and the release of methane (CH₄), a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential significantly higher than CO₂. By diverting manure from these conventional methods and instead processing it through a structured composting system, the project prevents methane emissions at source. The composting process stabilizes the organic material, producing high-quality compost that can be applied to agricultural land. This not only improves soil health and fertility but also enhances the soil’s carbon sequestration capacity, supporting long-term climate resilience in Romanian agriculture. In summary, the project delivers both immediate climate benefits through methane avoidance and broader environmental co-benefits by promoting sustainable manure management and improving local soil systems.

This is a Programme of Activities (PoA) called “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” in India that will include various Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs) in it. The “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” consists of implementation of Alternate and Wetting and Drying (AWD) practice in India. Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method and aerobic rice cultivation method is a scientifically proven way of managing rice fields for better water management and achieving reduction or avoidance of methane emissions that is caused in traditional submerged rice fields. Therefore, Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd. (an Indian entity) & WeAct Pty Ltd. (an Australian entity) has taken a voluntary initiative to develop a project in India that is designed specifically for Rice fields to adopt AWD and other adjusted water managements methods, to be implemented across various states of India. Thus, the main objective of the project is to avoid flooded irrigation in rice fields and adopt AWD/other adjusted water management methods for rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions from the rice fields.

The proposed project activity is the voluntary action undertaken by Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd., and WeAct Pty Ltd. The project falls under the Agriculture category introducing improved agricultural practices in rice cultivation. This project aims to reduce methane (CH4) emissions through improved water management practices involving alternate wetting and drying (AWD) of the paddy lands. AWD is a proven method to reduce CH4 emission by as much as 48% compared to continuously flooded conditions where high rates of CH4 are emitted by the lands due to the anaerobic decomposition of the organic matter . Rice is the most prominent food crop in India. It is the backbone of livelihood for millions of rural households and plays a vital role in the country’s food security. India is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of rice and hence plays an important part in the country’s economy. The proposed VPA activity is planned to be implemented in the Madhya Pradesh State of India. This VPA is implemented in Seoni district covering 26,103 ha in 8 tahsils

The proposed Programme of Activities (PoA) involves the production of biomass briquettes, with the objective of replacing conventional fossil fuels such as coal, furnace oil, and firewood commonly used by industries and institutions for thermal energy applications. The primary goal is to promote the use of clean, renewable, and sustainable biomass energy while reducing reliance on carbon-intensive fuels. Each Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) under this PoA will involve the manufacture of briquettes using agricultural residues and other organic biomass waste, which are typically discarded or left to decompose, resulting in methane emissions and environmental degradation. By converting this waste into high-density fuel briquettes, the PoA addresses key environmental and economic challenges. It contributes to greenhouse gas emission reductions by displacing fossil fuels and preventing methane emissions from un-managed biomass waste. The initiative also supports improved waste management through the productive use of agricultural residues, offers access to cleaner-burning fuels for small and medium-sized industrial units, and generates local employment across the biomass value chain—from raw material collection and processing to transportation and distribution. Additionally,by reducing the use of coal and wood, the PoA helps improve air quality and public health through lower emissions of particulate matter and other harmful pollutants.

The PoA aims to reduce methane emissions from irrigated paddy fields by implementing the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technique. Additionally, AWD offers a variety of socio-economic and environmental advantages. It allows farmers to decrease water consumption while maintaining crop yields, thereby improving water management and enhancing overall water access. The VPA aims to reduce methane emissions from irrigated paddy fields by implementing the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technique. Unlike traditional continuous flooding methods, AWD involves intermittent flooding, allowing fields to dry at certain intervals. This approach significantly reduces methane production while also lowering water consumption, making it both environmentally, socially and economically beneficial. In addition to promoting AWD, the VPA will support participating farmers with a comprehensive package of best practices tailored to optimize rice cultivation in the region.

BIWACALI stands for Burka Initiative for Water Balancing, Carbon Sequestration and Livelihood Improvement. The Oromo word “Burquaa” means “burbling spring”, symbolizing the main objective of this project: ensuring the water security of the West-Ethiopian Upper Dabana - and the East-Ethiopian Hakim Gara watersheds by restoring about 10,000 ha areas degraded area into forest over the next decades. This will be achieved by tree planting and applying the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) technique, which is designed to significantly improve the income and livelihoods of local farming communities. Next to the physical restoration work, major project activities are the formation of cooperatives and unions for forest management and training on FMNR, sustainable farming methods and alternative livelihoods. The newly created cooperatives will be strongly supported by World Vision Ethiopia in the first years of the project. It is envisioned that afterwards, they will take on the main responsibility for managing the forest areas, their products and the monitoring of the project impacts. The project is being implemented jointly by the local communities, Heineken Ethiopia, World Vision Ethiopia and FORLIANCE.

The Programme of Activities (PoA), titled 'Sustainable Rice Production in South East and South Asia', is a multi-country initiative that promotes the adoption of a suite of sustainable agricultural practices. The project's core measure is Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate-smart irrigation technique aimed at reducing methane emissions and conserving water in rice fields. While initial implementation is focused on rice-growing regions in Indonesia and Vietnam, the project is designed with a long-term vision to scale across other countries in South and Southeast Asia. The primary goal is to generate quantifiable carbon and water benefits, with a broader aim to improve the overall environmental and social sustainability of rice farming by incorporating measures that address soil health, energy efficiency, and pollution control.

The VPA for Indonesia, a foundational component of the overarching PoA, focuses on promoting sustainable rice production. The project's core activity is the implementation of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) to reduce methane emissions and conserve water. Serving as the primary pilot for the Rize business model, the VPA leverages a digital platform and on-ground technical support to ensure effective AWD adoption among smallholder farmers. The project aims to improve yields, reduce input costs, and generate a verifiable carbon asset stream that contributes to Indonesia's climate commitments while providing additional income for participating farmers.

The project's core activity is the implementation of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) to reduce methane emissions and conserve water. By providing farmers with training and technical support, the VPA aims to improve yields, reduce input costs, and create a verifiable carbon asset stream that contributes to the country's climate commitments and generates additional income for participating farmers.

This will displace a proportion of the fossil fuel that the factories currently burn.

The project activity includes realization of solar powered safe drinking water systems situated in the Afar, East Hararghe, Somali, Guji and Gumuz regions. The project seeks to promote agroforestry in rural areas of India. The project's focus is to improve livelihood of the farmer community by enhancing their social and economic status. The project will not only remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere but will also help in building climate resilience among the farming community. The agroforestry system will improve soil fertility, reduce erosion, enhance water retention, and increase resilience to climate shocks such as drought and flooding. The project avoids environmental degradation by reducing synthetic fertilizer dependency and preventing land degradation.

This project will be implemented in the Mozambican provinces of Inhambane and Gaza, reaching local communities that rely on traditional biomass fuels for cooking. Its central strategy is the promotion and deployment of improved charcoal and firewood cookstoves (ICS), aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and generate environmental, social, and economic benefits aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Implementation will be led by TDH Germany (project owner) and MAHLAHLE (local implementer), combining international standards with local knowledge for effective delivery. The project will deploy 9,000 charcoal ICS, all compliant with Gold Standard requirements and locally manufactured or assembled at a dedicated facility. These stoves will increase combustion efficiency, reduce indoor air pollution, cut emissions, and lower household energy costs. Over the first five-year crediting period, the project is expected to reduce 81,000 tons of CO₂e, based on Gold Standard TPDDTEC methodology. Designed to deliver multiple co-benefits, it contributes to SDG13 (climate action through 81,000 tCO₂e reductions), SDG15 (forest conservation), and SDG3 (better health from cleaner air). Socially, it advances SDG3 (reduced smoke exposure), SDG4 (environmental clubs for climate literacy), SDG5 (gender equality through time savings for women), and SDG6 (improved sanitation via water systems). Economically, it supports SDG1 (lower household fuel expenses), SDG7 (cleaner cooking for 9,000 households), and SDG8 (job creation in production, distribution, and education).

The Durable Solutions Congo: Clean energy and environmental resilience in the DRC, is a Programme of Activities (PoA) whose purpose is to improve access to efficient cookstoves and safe water supply technologies for low-income households in rural and peri-urban areas throughout the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The technologies distributed under this PoA aim to address pressing environmental, health and social challenges in a locally appropriate manner. Serving as the starting point, the real-case VPA intends to contribute towards the goals of the PoA by distributing the “Sala Makala Stove,” a Top-Lit Up-Draft (TLUD) stove capable of combusting firewood more efficiently than traditional/3-stone biomass cookstoves. Thereby saving approximately 2.04 tCO2e per household per year. The project further aims to improve air quality and subsequently, household health, by reducing exposure to harmful smoke, as well as reducing fuelwood consumption with greater stove efficiency.

The FS BECCS project, proposed under the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG), reflects FS – Fueling Sustainability’s ambition to lead Brazil’s energy transition with innovation, technical excellence, and private investment. Founded in 2017, FS is the third-largest ethanol producer in the country, operating modern plants in Mato Grosso. At its Lucas do Rio Verde facility, FS will capture biogenic CO₂ from corn ethanol fermentation. The stream, with about 98% purity, will be compressed, dehydrated, and injected into deep geological formations of the Parecis Basin for secure, long-term storage. As this CO₂ originates from the atmosphere via photosynthesis, its storage delivers net carbon removals. Project development followed four phases: Phase 1 (2019–2020) confirmed storage potential through feasibility studies and 2D seismic data. Phase 2 (2020–2022) added a 3D seismic survey and design of capture and compression systems. Phase 3 (2022–2024) drilled a stratigraphic well, collected geological data, and began equipment procurement. Phase 4 (2024–2026), now underway, includes injectivity tests, well conversion, monitoring infrastructure, and capture system construction. Commercial operations are expected in 2025, with carbon injection June 2026.

The MuLaKiLa project is a long-term (32 years) community-based landscape restoration and climate resilience initiative in Rwanda’s western province, spanning Ngororero and Rutsiro districts. As part of the voluntary carbon market, it is projected to sequester 5.4 million tons of CO₂e, with 4.356 million tons of CO₂e accounted for after buffer deduction. The project will restore 21,000 hectares of degraded smallholder land through agroforestry systems, woodlots, and Sustainable Agriculture Land Management (SALM) practices. It will benefit around 160,000 farmers by creating green jobs, improving livelihoods, and addressing climate challenges such as soil erosion, land degradation, and biodiversity loss. Core interventions include planting over 6 million trees, community mobilization, capacity building, and the establishment of innovative nature-based financial mechanisms.

The Future Radici Programme of Activities (PoA) represents a voluntary, long-term climate and biodiversity initiative developed and managed by Leone Alato SpA, the Coordinating and Managing Entity (CME). It has been conceived as an afforestation and reforestation (A/R) programme to address the interlinked crises of climate change, biodiversity degradation, and ecosystem loss. By planting native, long-cycle, non-invasive trees within the Leone Alato perimeter (Italy end Romania), the overarching aim is to contribute substantively to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with a principal focus on SDG 13 (Climate Action) through the biological removal and long-term storage of atmospheric carbon dioxide via A/R practices. In doing so, the PoA also contributes to SDG 15 (Life on Land) through the restoration of degraded ecosystems and the strengthening of biodiversity, as well as to SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) by reducing synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, and SDG 5 (Gender Equality) by generating inclusive and equitable socioeconomic opportunities within local communities.

The Real Case VPA Future Radici, Lanuvio represents a pivotal and strategic initiative within the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) Future Radici. Located in the municipality of Lanuvio (Rome), the project spans a total area of 403.9 hectares across three agricultural estates: Solonio, Presciano, and Campoleone. These lands are owned by Leone Alato SpA. The project envisions the planting of approximately 422,000 trees, with the goal of transforming these agricultural lands into thriving, biodiverse forest ecosystems. The primary objective of the Real Case of Lanuvio is to establish native and ecologically rich forest environments through a combination of afforestation and agroforestry practices. These practices are carefully tailored to the pedoclimatic and ecological characteristics of each site, ensuring that the interventions enhance biodiversity, support complex habitats, and maximize long-term carbon sequestration. The forest models adopted in this project are non-extractive, the harvesting of timber or biomass is explicitly excluded. This commitment extends for a minimum duration of 60 years. To quantify the carbon absorption, the project will rely on methodologies recommended by the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). These methods will be calibrated using national and regional data. The goal is to produce credits that are measurable, verifiable, and directly linked to positive outcomes in both biodiversity and social impact.

This project introduces Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) as a climate-smart water management practice in rice farming in Dong Thap Province, a major rice-producing area of the Mekong Delta. The project aims to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation, save irrigation water, and support sustainable rice production. It is being implemented by Rikolto in Vietnam acting on behalf of Livelihoods Carbon Fund (LCF3). The core technical intervention of the project is the application of AWD, a water-saving irrigation technique that reduces methane emissions in rice cultivation. Instead of keeping rice paddies continuously flooded, AWD involves allowing the field to dry intermittently, typically until the water level drops 15 cm below the soil surface, at which point irrigation is resumed with a shallow flood of 2–5 cm. This practice reduces the anaerobic conditions in the soil that are responsible for methane generation, without negatively affecting rice yields. To support this method, the project installs PVC monitoring tubes (commonly known as pani-pipes) in farmers’ fields. These tools allow farmers to visually monitor the water level in the soil and make informed irrigation decisions, making AWD both accessible and easy to implement. In addition to water management, the project promotes improved straw and fertilizer practices. Rather than incorporating straw into the soil, which significantly contributes to methane emissions, farmers are encouraged to remove, compost, or repurpose straw for other uses such as mushroom cultivation. Fertilizer use is also optimized to improve nitrogen efficiency and reduce emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O), another potent greenhouse gas.

This Gold Standard Large-Scale (Individual) Project Activity is a voluntary initiative developed by Clean Cooking Technologies S.R.L. (CCT) as the Project Developer. The project will be supported by multiple investors and funding partners. The Host Country for this project is the United Republic of Tanzania, where the activity will be implemented across the country. The project aims to distribute high-quality induction stoves and electric pressure cookers (collectively referred to as electric cookstoves) to households and communities in Tanzania. Implementation will be led by CCT Tanzania, in collaboration with local organizations. The project will initially be rolled out in Dar es Salaam and subsequently expanded to other regions across Tanzania based on demand. In Tanzania, a large proportion of households continue to rely on inefficient traditional cooking methods—such as three-stone fires and traditional charcoal stoves—that consume significant amounts of biomass and contribute to deforestation and indoor air pollution. By introducing modern, energy-efficient electric cooking technologies, the project seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve indoor air quality, and enhance the overall quality of life for participating households. The project will be implemented in both rural and urban areas where households have access to electricity. The project will have a total crediting period of 15 years, comprising an initial 5-year period with two renewals of 5 years each. 100 of % distributed induction stoves in the project will be equipped with IoT devices to enable continuous monitoring of energy consumption for cooking and water heating in the households. The project will apply the Gold Standard-approved methodology, "Methodology for Metered & Measured Energy Cooking Devices" (Version 1.2), recognized as the most robust and conservative emission reduction calculation approach for cookstove carbon projects. This methodology is also endorsed by the ICVCM under its Core Carbon Principles (CCP), ensuring transparency and integrity in carbon credit issuance from cookstove projects. By combining energy-efficient modern elelctric cookstove technology with real-time usage monitoring using the latest IoT device and a rigorous Gold Standard Metered Methodology, and further fNRB value derived from MoFUSS for Tanzania, the project will generate high-quality, high-integrity carbon credits while avoiding any risk of overestimation. The project is also one of the approved project by Sylvera. Beyond emissions reduction, the project is designed to deliver substantial co-benefits aligned with many UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including: - SDG 1: No Poverty - SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being - SDG 4: Quality Education - SDG 5: Gender Equality - SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy - SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth - SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production - SDG 13: Climate Action - SDG 15: Life on Land These co-benefits will be formally certified under the Gold Standard framework, reinforcing the project's holistic impact on climate and community resilience.

Carbon Neutral Energy Systems Limited (C-NES) has developed the "Ecofoyer Guinée - Programme for the Dissemination of Improved and Advanced Cookstoves in Guinea" as a registered Gold Standard Programme of Activities (PoA). The PoA reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improves household well-being by displacing the use of traditional, inefficient biomass cookstoves with modern, energy-efficient and cleaner alternatives. The PoA responds to Guinea’s NDCs and its significant dependence on traditional cooking practices, which has resulted in widespread deforestation, indoor air pollution, and associated health burdens—especially among women and children. Through the introduction of improved cookstoves (ICS), advanced cookstoves (ACS), and local manufacturing of renewable fuels (biomass pellets) the Ecofoyer Guinée PoA contributes to sustainable energy access, climate mitigation, and social development across urban, peri-urban and rural areas. Under this country-wide PoA, the initial rollout includes the prefectures of Conakry, N’Zérékoré, Forécariah, and Beyla. The PoA involves the dissemination, monitoring, and maintenance of ICS and ACS technologies that meet defined efficiency and emission performance standards.

The primary beneficiaries are households that currently cook with biomass but are already connected to the national grid. Uduma's Safe Water Program provides safe water to rural communities in Western Africa with the first carbon project beginning in Mali. Uduma installs low-emission water treatment technologies (in-line chlorination) to existing water supply systems, maintains the systems, and expands systems to reach those in need. The resulting safe water replaces the need to burn non-renewable biomass in water boiling for purification. This avoidance of fuel combustion reduces Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions and positively contributes to climate change goals and sustainable development goals.
