The goal of the “Community Program for the Preservation and Restoration of Mangroves” is to implement projects for the restoration of degraded mangrove and coastal/freshwater wetlands ecosystems. The aim is to recover ecological functionality by re-establishing hydrological connectivity, improving biodiversity, and removing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) through natural carbon sequestration processes. VPAs included under the PoA will be selected where degradation is demonstrated and restoration is technically feasible, prioritizing actions such as hydrological reconnection, assisted natural regeneration, and targeted enrichment planting with native species, together with the maintenance and monitoring required for durable outcomes. The aim is to restore ecological processes (water exchange, sediment dynamics, recruitment), enhance biodiversity, and remove CO₂ through conservative, verified sequestration in line with Gold Standard requirements.

The "Mangrove Restoration Project of 500 Hectares" is the first of several expected voluntary project activities (VPAs) to be included under the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) “Community Program for the Preservation and Restoration of Mangroves”. The project consists of the ecological restoration of 500.87 hectares of degraded mangrove ecosystems. The total project area consists of 500.87 ha, out of which 431.14 ha are eligible (degraded and transitional mangrove). Restoration measures include the reconnection of blocked tidal channels and removal of sediment plugs, assisted natural regeneration where hydrological conditions permit, and enrichment planting with native species.

The GETPP Digital MRV Programme of Activities (PoA) for Clean Energy, Productive Use & Community Restoration in Nigeria is a nationwide programme deploying climate-smart energy and land-use interventions across households, schools, SMEs, cooperatives, and communities. The PoA includes five activity categories: (1) LED lighting efficiency upgrades; (2) distributed solar and hybrid inverter systems; (3) replacement of diesel/petrol generators with solar and battery systems; (4) productive-use clean energy technologies, including energy-efficient equipment and biogas-based clean cooking solutions; and (5) tree planting, agroforestry, and environmental restoration. The programme is supported by a digital MRV system featuring GPS-tagged, timestamped evidence, metadata validation, user-level activity tracking, and automated QA/QC processes, generating audit-ready monitoring reports. The system supports both direct and assisted (proxy) participation, ensuring inclusion of stakeholders without reliable internet access. The PoA aims to reduce GHG emissions, support carbon sequestration, improve energy access, eliminate fossil-fuel generators, support Nigeria’s NDCs, strengthen livelihoods, and promote sustainable behavioural change.

Chishang, nestled in Taitung County, Taiwan, is renowned as a premier rice production region with a legacy of more than 70 years. The area’s lush paddies and traditional agricultural rhythms are stewarded by the Wanan Community Development Association (WACDA), an active local group established three decades ago. WACDA’s mission centers on environmental protection, cultural conservation, and the promotion of organic farming—principles that have guided community action and land management for generations. Typical farming practices in Chishang after the second rice harvest in late October include thorough removal of litter and several rounds of tillage, followed by maintaining clear, fallow fields until February. This period of rest for the land helps sanitize soil-borne disease bacteria. However, to manage weeds during this time, herbicides have traditionally been applied, reflecting both pragmatic and conventional approaches to field management. In recent years, Chishang’s farmers, under WACDA’s leadership, have begun to embrace more sustainable soil management techniques. Inspired by the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG) Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the community has adopted Cover Crops and Improved Tillage Activity Modules. These practices promise enhanced outcomes for both food security and climate resilience, by increasing soil carbon, reducing chemical use, and supporting ecosystem health.

Overview The US SecondCropTM Microbial Carbon Removal project represents a pioneering approach in agriculture-based carbon removal and is centered around the use of proprietary microbial technology to improve soil health and drive long-term carbon sequestration. The project transforms conventional farmland into durable carbon sinks by enhancing stable soil carbon, producing measurable climate and soil health outcomes. A key innovation in this program is the deployment of CarbonBuilderTM, a proprietary microbial inoculant developed by Loam Bio (refer to Appendix 5 - CarbonBuilder Development Stages at Loam Bio for a detailed summary of the product development pipeline). CarbonBuilder is applied as a seed treatment to enhance plant fertility, promote soil health, and increase the sequestration of soil organic carbon by reintroducing beneficial fungi into the soil. The US SecondCrop Microbial Carbon Removal project represents a grouped project comprising 36 farms. Participating farms are located in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, South Dakota and Wisconsin with a median farm size of 550 acres. All farms in the project are historically and currently used for cropping, primarily under a corn-soy rotation. Prior to the implementation of this project, there were no equivalent initiatives in the region focused on stable soil organic carbon sequestration. Agricultural practices in the U.S. Midwest were predominantly conventional, characterized by routine tillage and heavy reliance on synthetic fertilizers. The baseline scenario assumes the continuation of these practices in the absence of the project, leading to higher emissions and declining soil resilience over time. Under the project, participating farmers apply CarbonBuilder to applicable crops each year at the time of planting. Unlike conventional soil carbon projects that depend only on practice changes (no-till, cover crops), Loam’s inoculant accelerates microbial-fungal-root interactions that channel plant carbon into mineral- associated organic matter (MAOM) and aggregate-associated organic matter. Building stronger soil health in agricultural landscapes within United States Regenerative agricultural practices hold immense potential for higher adoption rates among farmers in the U.S. Midwest, a region characterized by its flat topography and fertile mollisol soils that are ideal for large-scale, mechanized farming (USDA NRCS). Historically, conventional farming in this area has relied on intensive tillage and heavy use of synthetic fertilizers to maximize yields. However, this has led to higher emissions and declining soil resilience over time. A study in the journal Earth's Future found that agricultural fields in the Midwestern U.S. have lost an average of two millimeters of soil per year since Euro-American settlement, nearly double the rate the USDA considers sustainable. It has been estimated that over the last 160 years, the region has lost approximately 57.6 trillion metric tons of topsoil, with plowing activities cited as the major culprit (Thaler et al. 2022). Similarly, research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) revealed that the Midwest Corn Belt has lost its topsoil (A-horizon soil) from roughly one-third of its cultivated area, a significantly higher estimate than previous soil surveys indicated. This soil loss has removed 1.4 ± 0.5 petagrams of carbon from hillslopes, reducing crop yields in the study area by around 6% and causing billions in annual economic losses (Thaler et al. 2021). Poor soil health has a significant impact on productivity and the broader agricultural economy. The shift to regenerative practices including reduced or no-tillage, cover cropping, and the use of bio-stimulants, is therefore crucial for improving soil health, enhancing water retention, and mitigating climate change through potential widespread carbon removal and long-term sequestration. The proposed project activity aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions at the Lam Thach Cement Plant through the introduction of alternative fuels and clinker optimization measures. The project will replace a portion of fossil fuels traditionally used in the cement kiln with waste-derived fuels such as refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and dewatered sludge, which would otherwise be landfilled or improperly disposed. This substitution reduces CO₂ emissions associated with fossil fuel combustion and supports improved waste management practices. In addition, the project will lower process emissions by decreasing the clinker-to-cement ratio through the increased use of suitable supplementary cementitious materials. This results in reduced calcination-related CO₂ emissions from clinker production. The combined interventions contribute to a significant reduction in the carbon intensity of cement manufacturing at Lam Thach. The initiative supports Vietnam’s climate and circular economy objectives by diverting waste from landfills, reducing fossil fuel dependence, and promoting more efficient resource use. The overall project activity contributes to regional and national sustainable development.

The solar power project in the Benban region of Egypt aims to generate clean electricity from renewable solar energy and supply it to the national grid. With its substantial installed capacity, the project will contribute to Egypt’s transition towards sustainable energy systems and supports national efforts to reduce reliance on fossil fuel–based power generation.

Green Mining's PoA is based on operationalizing the collection, transportation, and destination of waste for recycling. In doing so, the PoA promotes the circular economy and prevents the environmental impacts of manufacturing new products from virgin material, ensuring greater energy efficiency in the production process and, thus, reducing associated Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions. The PoA is located in Brazil, and its operations are organized around receiving centers strategically placed in areas with high post-consumer waste generation. These centers receive, weigh, and properly store waste brought by registered local waste pickers, providing them fair compensation in a way that prioritizes the social inclusion of people in vulnerable situations. In this regard, the PoA stands out for its disruptive nature, passing on the full value of waste to registered waste pickers and expanding the positive social impact of recycling. Once properly registered, the waste is transported to the plants responsible for the recycling process, ensuring its subsequent reinsertion into the production chain. This PoA constitutes, therefore, an overarching framework aimed at promoting recycling in Brazil in an inclusive and sustainable manner.

OffgridSun Srl and Istituto Oikos Ets have partnered to distribute improved cookstoves (ICS) in Longido District in the Arusha region to reduce the reliance on firewood and charcoal of the local population. The CDR ORINOQUÍA project, developed by Biofix Consultoría S.A.S BIC, is a large-scale afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation (ARR) initiative designed to mitigate climate change by restoring degraded savannah ecosystems in the Orinoco region of Colombia. The project covers 8,441 hectares across seven private properties (Arizona, La Fortuna, La Carolina, San Andrés, Villa Claudia, Buenos Aires, and San Miguel) located in Puerto Gaitán, Meta. The project employs a dual reforestation strategy: Forest Plantations: Establishment of non-native species (Eucalyptus pellita and Pinus caribaea). Natural Enrichment: Restoration of non-flood zones and flooded areas (gallery and moriche forests) using native species such as Cassia grandis, Hymenaea courbaril, Caraipa llanorum, Mauritia flexuosa, Euterpe precatoria, and Manilkara zapota. To achieve its goals, the project operates a permanent nursery producing over three million seedlings annually. Implementation includes specialized machinery for site preparation, alongside GPS and drone technology for precise monitoring. This integrated approach aims to increase carbon sequestration and generate certified carbon credits while contributing to SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 15 (Life on Land). The project boundary encompasses all land parcels dedicated to these ARR activities as GHG sinks.

The core project facilities consist of a waste logistics and aggregation unit where recyclable materials collected by local waste pickers are received, weighed, sorted, temporarily stored and transported to recycling plants, from which they are reintroduced into the production chain.

The purpose of the project is to install heat pumps in Kyrgyzstan. Heat pumps are modern devices used in heating, air conditioning and hot water applications. Unlike other heat generators (coal, gas, diesel and electric), the heat pump extracts (pumps out) low-potential energy from the environment (accumulated during the warm season from ground, groundwater, rocks etc) and increases the heat potential by transferring heat energy from a source with a lower temperature to a higher temperature via the thermodynamic steam-compression cycle. Heat pumps needs an external energy source, usually electricity, to operate. The most common design of a heat pump consists of a compressor, a thermal expansion valve, an evaporator and a condenser. The coolant circulating inside these components is called refrigerant. The project involves the installation of Heat pumps in its first phase in Bishkek and Chuy Region. These HPs replace energy-intensive heating solutions used in homes, and institutions which run on carbon-intensive and expensive fossil fuels.

The objective of the program is to support smallholder farmers and rural communities in adopting sustainable agroforestry practices, which involve planting trees alongside crops or on fallow land across India. In addition to the economic benefits, the project will also reduce vulnerability to climate change. By increasing tree cover, it will help combat land degradation, improve water retention, and enhance biodiversity. Furthermore, the program will provide farmers access to carbon credit revenue share, promoting sustainable land use while improving their long-term livelihoods

Smart Train Lease offers the opportunity to rent innovative, sustainable, state-of-the-art battery trains which can replace diesel trains. Mireo Smart trains are part of the leasing model of Smart Train Lease. They are available in various versions but for this project activity the focus is on the highly energy-efficient battery-electric train (referred to as “Plus B”). The battery train fleet is managed centrally and enables rail operators to rent trains at short notice, offering a cost-efficient solution for regional passenger transport services, depending on the demand. production, lease and monitoring of 24 Mireo Smart Plus B across Germany, starting from 2026. The ultimate purpose of Smart Train Lease is to displace old diesel trains, contributing to the cleaner, greener, and smarter mobility transition in Germany by aligning with sustainable development goals, resulting in a reduction of 10,334 tCO2e on average per year and a total of 51,672 tCO2e over the first crediting period of 5 years from 01/07/2026 to 30/06/2031.

BIOPLANTATION is undertaking an agroforestry project in collaboration with local communities in Ghana. The project activity aims to restore degraded, under utilized land by developing biodiverse, regenerative agro forests. These forests will help combat climate change, support food security and create local jobs. The project will include Moringa Oleifera, a fast-growing and climate-resilient tree and associated species, along with local crops like peanuts and native species, to regenerate soil, store carbon, and support local livelihoods. BIOPLANTATION will bring together proven techniques, in a modular and regenerative design, that can be replicated and scaled up to different communities in Ghana. Planting of trees and crops including Moringa, peanuts, native fruits, fire/windbreak species, and aromatic plants. Soil restoration and regeneration will be through nitrogen-fixing plants and organic matter. Enhancing indigenous biodiversity will be by allocating 10% of project land to support pollination, biodiversity, and honey production. BIOPLANTATION Ghana is committed to working in close partnership with local communities. During all phases of planning, implementation, and monitoring, community feedback and participation will be prioritized. The project will offer training, ownership, and income opportunities to local residents.

69% of Lesotho’s population live rurally and cook on open fires. Cooking this way is hugely consumptive of wood, water and time. The purpose of the project is to reduce the negative impacts of cooking using biomass in Lesotho. Traditional foods such as beans require long cooking times, meaning large amounts of wood. A typical Lesotho household cooks continuously for 5 hours each day. Fuel wood harvesting is hard, tiring and repetitive work often done by young women. This limits opportunities for education and independence, and exposes women to risk of assault. Harvesting also impacts local habitats and exposes soil to irreversible erosion. Water must also be collected, much of which is lost during the traditional cooking process. In partnership with local women, we are making heat retention cooking bags. Instead of hours of continuous cooking, the bag only requires the cook to bring food to the boil then place the hot lidded pot into the bag. This reduces cooking time from hours to 25 minutes. 79% less fuel wood is required, equating to CO2e reduction of around two tonnes per bag per year. 80% less water is required as water no longer boils away during cooking, which also means nutrients are not lost, improving the nutritional value of the food. Ultimately, the cook saves 1500 hours per year. It is no overstatement to say this changed lives in our pilot program. Women began craft making, trained to manufacture the Eco Cook Bags, or are growing and selling food.

This project aims to mechanically process large-format steel plates (up to 2 t) from industrial dismantling without melting them down. The plates are restored to a technically flawless condition through straightening, flame cutting, and sandblasting, and are then reintroduced to the market as construction steel. In contrast to conventional recycling methods that rely on energy-intensive melting processes (e.g., blast furnaces or electric arc furnaces (EAF)), this project creates 'Reuse Steel' through a purely mechanical process. This approach avoids a significant portion of the energy and CO2 intensity associated with conventional steel production. The resulting Reuse Steel can be a substitute for various steel applications across construction or infrastructure components (non-structural).

Reducing Methane Emissions through Improved Rice Cultivation in India Program of Activities (PoA), developed by Commonland B.V., aims to address one of the key sources of greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture: methane from rice farming. The POA aims to promote sustainable cultivation practices through promoting Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), as alternatives to conventional continuous flooding. By improving water management and soil conditions, the PoA seeks to reduce methane emissions, enhance climate resilience, and support farmer livelihoods across different regions of India.

The rice cultivation project in Kabirdham, India, is a joint effort between Commonland B.V. and Chhattisgarh Agricon Private Limited, aimed at promoting sustainable agricultural practices while reducing methane emissions. The initiative encourages farmers to adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) techniques to replace conventional continuous flooding, which is a major source of methane emissions in rice farming. By improving water management and soil conditions, this project seeks to enhance agricultural sustainability and farmer livelihoods.

Transformation of degraded land in Extremadura, Spain into cork oak estates. This project is the first in a series of future projects that will be grouped by annual cohorts. The baseline scenario is that traditional cork oak woodlands are under serious threats from climate change, fragile ecosystems, lack of management, wildfires as well as biotic and abiotic stresses. There is almost no incentive to plant new cork oak trees due to the very long time horizon. Cork oak estates increase the ecosystem value of the land, providing valuable habitats for native species, reducing erosion, and preserving the soil structure, increasing water holding and storing capacity as well as increasing shades. Degraded land is often used for non-permanent pastures, leading to desertification.

The project aims to restore 791 hectares of degraded land in the north-eastern section of Kibale National Park, Uganda. Following heavy encroachment in the past century, the area was abandoned but natural forest regeneration remains severely constrained by elephant grass and recurring fires. Without active intervention, forest recovery would not occur. The project site is located in the mid-eastern part of Kibale National Park in Kyenjojo District, Western Uganda, and borders communities largely dependent on smallholder agriculture and affected by land scarcity, human–wildlife conflict, and pressure on natural resources. Restoration will focus on active reforestation using indigenous tree species, including nursery establishment, seedling production and planting, weeding, fire prevention, patrolling, and long-term maintenance. Community members will be engaged through employment opportunities. Complementary activities will address human–wildlife conflict, support alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping, piggery, and agroforestry, and promote environmental awareness. Without the project, the area would remain dominated by elephant grass and frequent fires, resulting in low carbon storage, limited biodiversity recovery, and soil degradation. The project changes this trajectory by enabling large-scale forest restoration, improving habitat quality, increasing carbon sequestration, and delivering socio-economic benefits to neighbouring communities.

The Maldives Captive Solar Photovoltaic Renewable Energy Project involves the installation and operation of stand-alone rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) systems at captive consumer facilities across the Maldives. The solar PV systems generate renewable electricity exclusively for on-site consumption. The project directly replaces electricity that would otherwise be produced using diesel-based generators, which are the primary source of power for captive and isolated facilities in the Maldives.

The Water for Planet Initiative recognizes that households across Rwanda are still relying on unsafe water sources for their water needs and that to make the water safe, most resort to treatment by boiling with non-renewable biomass resulting into GHG Emissions. The Project will provide safe water to communities in Rwanda by installing water treatment technologies (in-line chlorination) to existing community water supply (CWS) systems. The project will also maintain the system, expand piped water access, and provide regular water quality monitoring and awareness within the communities. The resulting safe water access and public awareness of its safety is likely to replace the need to burn non-renewable biomass in water treatment through boiling. This will result in reduced GHG emissions and positively contribute to climate change goals and sustainable development goals.

The B4H Initiative is a sustainable energy project aimed at promoting renewable energy and waste management in rural households across two Indian states. The initiative involves the installation of 14,690 household biogas plants, primarily in Maharashtra (13,752 units) and Madhya Pradesh (938 units). These plants utilize animal dung to generate biogas for thermal energy, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. The project adheres to the "Methodology for Animal Manure Management and Biogas Use for Thermal Energy Generation" (Version 1.1, released January 25, 2023). The Household biogas units are sized at 2m³ , 3m³ , and 4m³, enabling clean cooking and organic fertilizer production for beneficiaries. By addressing methane emissions from manure and providing affordable energy, B4H enhances livelihoods, improves air quality, and supports climate resilience in underserved communities. The initiative targets rural farmers, with installations verified through a detailed beneficiary database,to ensure long-term monitoring for carbon credit issuance.

The Proyecto Forestal Los Tualdos (Los Tualdos) is an environmental initiative aimed at transforming 204 hectares of degraded grassland by establishing sustainable forest plantations composed of both native and exotic species. By planting more than 152,000 trees and restoring local ecosystems, the project is expected to sequester approximately 105,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent over the next three decades.

The main objectives of this project are to provide water treatment to schools in Rwanda to address microbiological contamination, and avoid CO2e emissions associated with water treatment. The water purification systems will reduce both the use of and demand for firewood and other fuels used to boil drinking water, leading to the reduction of carbon dioxide emissions. The voluntary project activity (VPA) is a voluntary initiative by Unlocking Communities (UC) to distribute improved charcoal stoves in Haiti. The target beneficiaries under the project will be the households which were earlier dependent on charcoal based traditional stoves for cooking. Unlocking Communities is a locally run organization working in northern and central Haiti. Distribution of improved cookstove which is a clean energy product as compared to the baseline, will reduce the GHG emissions. The use of improved cookstove will offer several environmental and health benefits such as reduction in the levels of indoor air pollution (IAP), women drudgery, deforestation etc. thereby having a positive impact on the health of the community.

This real-case VPA is implemented under the GETPP Digital MRV Programme of Activities (GS23489) and covers community-level clean energy and land-use interventions in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria. The VPA deploys CPA-linked activities across households, farmers, and SMEs, including LED lighting replacement, distributed solar and mini-grid systems, and replacement of diesel/petrol generators with solar and battery systems. The VPA also includes productive-use energy technologies for agriculture and small enterprises, as well as biogas-based clean cooking solutions. In addition, afforestation, agroforestry, and environmental restoration activities are implemented to support carbon sequestration and land rehabilitation. All activities are monitored through a digital MRV system incorporating GPS-tagged, timestamped evidence, metadata validation, and activity-level verification. The system supports both direct and assisted participation to ensure inclusion of stakeholders without reliable internet access, while ensuring transparency, traceability, and compliance with Gold Standard requirements.

The IRIBA Water Access Program in Rwanda (IWAP Rwanda) is a transformative climate and health initiative bringing clean, carbon-free drinking water to underserved schools and communities across Rwanda. Implemented by IRIBA Water Group, the program will install 2,500 smart water ATMs providing safe, affordable drinking water to over 1 million people who need it most. These innovative water points eliminate the need to boil water with firewood or charcoal, directly reducing greenhouse gas emissions while preventing deforestation and improving public health.

The Kuphatana project aims to reforest 1,000 hectares of highly degraded land in the Administrative Post of Murraça, Mozambique, to restore the local ecosystem and support the socio-economic development of nearby communities. The project adopts a participatory approach, integrating environmental restoration with diversified livelihood activities such as beekeeping and dried mango production to ensure long-term sustainability and community engagement. Climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions Carbon Sequestration: The project establishes a forest that serves as a carbon sink, sequestering an annual average of 8,925 tCO2e. Over the 40-year crediting period, the total estimated net benefit is 351,044.5 tCO2e. Biodiversity Enhancement: By planting a mix of native species (Vachellia xanthophloea and Khaya anthotheca) alongside non-invasive Eucalyptus urophylla, the project restores habitats for local flora and fauna Climate Adaptation through Livelihoods - Beekeeping: The project engages 15 families per year from adjacent villages, providing them with beehives and training. This creates a direct economic incentive for the community to protect the forest from threats such as uncontrolled fires or illegal deforestation, as the bee colonies rely on the trees for nectar. Climate Adaptation through Livelihoods - Sustainable Value Chains: Establishing a local value chain for dried mangoes offers diversified, climate-resilient financial growth for local families.

The project aims to support the energy transition and reduce charcoal consumption and related greenhouse gas emissions through the distribution of improved charcoal cookstoves and pellet gasifier cookstoves within local communities. By promoting the adoption of cleaner and more efficient cooking technologies, the project contributes to lowering fuel demand, improving energy efficiency, and reducing environmental and climate impacts associated with traditional cooking practices. In parallel, the project places strong emphasis on community empowerment by creating local employment opportunities, delivering technical and operational training, and investing in essential community infrastructure such as water towers and greenhouses. These activities are designed to strengthen local capacities, improve access to resources, and foster sustainable socio-economic development in the countries where the project is implemented. The project contributes to the achievement of the following Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land).

The Gold Standard “Nestlé & FNC Tree Planting Colombia” is a joint strategy between Nestlé and the National Federation of Coffee Growers of Colombia (FNC). It is implemented through the planting of trees on coffee farms that are part of Nestlé’s value chain and on neighboring farms located within the coffee-growing ecosystem. The project emerged as a mitigation and adaptation measure to prepare crops for the impacts of climate variability, contribute to the conservation of water and soils, enhance biodiversity, and serve as a nature-based solution for the removal of CO₂ from the atmosphere.

UpEnergy Group will work with micro-entrepreneurs, NGOs, financial institutions, local distribution partners etc. to provide institutional users with safe drinking water systems. UpEnergy would ensure the last-mile distribution/installation of the clean technologies to the institutions. This VPA is implemented in host country-Federal Republic of Nigeria

This VPA aims to support the energy transition and reduce charcoal consumption and related greenhouse gas emissions through the distribution of improved charcoal cookstoves and pellet gasifier cookstoves, applying a fuel-switch approach. By promoting the adoption of cleaner and more efficient cooking solutions, the VPA contributes to reducing reliance on traditional charcoal and lowering associated environmental and climate impacts. The VPA will be implemented in Zambia, with a particular focus on the Copperbelt region, targeting urban and peri-urban areas. The activities are designed to generate positive impacts within local communities, with specific attention to supporting women’s empowerment through improved access to clean cooking technologies, reduced time spent on fuel collection, and enhanced livelihood opportunities. In addition, the VPA includes the construction of water towers to ensure reliable access to safe drinking water, along with continuous capacity-building activities aimed at strengthening local skills, knowledge, and long-term socio-economic resilience.

The voluntary project activity (VPA) is a voluntary initiative by Unlocking Communities (UC) to distribute institution water filters in Haiti. The target beneficiaries under the project will be the institutions like schools which were earlier dependent on boiling using non-renewable biomass for safe drinking water. Unlocking Communities is a locally run organization working in northern and central Haiti. The proposed GS project activity “CGR Guatapara Landfill Project” promotes destruction and utilization of landfill gas (LFG) (rich in methane) generated at the CGR Guatapará landfill, located in the municipality of Guatapará in São Paulo State (South-eastern region of Brazil). LFG destruction and utilization occurs through its collection and destruction in high temperature enclosed flare(s) and its utilization as gaseous fuel for electricity generation (in engine-generator sets installed at the CGR Guatapará landfill as part of the project activity) respectively. Thus, besides methane destruction, the project activity also promotes generation of electricity by using renewable energy source.

The proposed project activity aims to displace use of non-renewable fossil fuels such as fire wood, charcoal or LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) for cooking with clean cooking technologies such as biogas unit (biodigester and biogas stove) in the households of various states of India.

This project captures methane from vinasse generated during ethanol production through anaerobic digestion and converts the recovered biogas into renewable energy for on-site use. The project reduces greenhouse gas emissions by preventing uncontrolled methane release, displacing fossil fuel consumption, improving wastewater management, and contributing to sustainable industrial operations. The resulting emission reductions are eligible for certification under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals.

This VPA deploys efficient improved cookstoves (ICS), reducing woody biomass consumption for primarily rural households in the Republic of Malawi. The scenario existing prior to the implementation of the project is the use of very inefficient traditional cookstoves or 3- stone fires, consuming a lot of non-renewable charcoal and firewood. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils’ reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer.

The project activity titled “Proactiva CGA Iperó Landfill Gas to Energy Project” encompasses the promotion of destruction and utilization landfill gas (LFG) (rich in methane) at the CGA Iperó landfill site. LFG destruction occurs in a high temperature enclosed flare and through its utilization as gaseous fuel for electricity generation (in engine-generator sets). Thus, besides methane destruction, the project activity also promotes generation of electricity by using renewable energy sources (with a total nameplate capacity of about 8.5 MW). The CGA Iperó landfill is located located in the border of Sorocaba and Iperó’s municipalities, in São Paulo State, Southeastern Region of Brazil.

The Büyükkışla WPP Project with BESS is designed by Entek Elektrik Üretim A.Ş. as a strategic intervention to increase Türkiye’s renewable energy capacity while addressing the inherent stability challenges of wind power. The project activity involves the distribution and sustained use of improved cookstoves (ICS) to households in rural and peri-urban areas of Uganda, where traditional cooking practices predominantly rely on inefficient three-stone fires or rudimentary charcoal stoves. The primary objective of the project is to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by improving combustion efficiency and reducing the consumption of non-renewable biomass fuels, including firewood and charcoal. The project also aims to deliver co-benefits, including improved indoor air quality, reduced exposure to harmful pollutants, decreased pressure on local forest resources, and time savings for households, particularly benefiting women and children.

Insus B.V. implements a recycling process to recover and reuse waste polyurethane (PUR) insulation foam from construction and demolition activities. Traditionally, PUR insulation waste is landfilled or incinerated, leading to large numbers of greenhouse gas emissions. The project collects post-consumer and production PUR insulation waste and processes it into recycled raw material that is used in the production of new green insulation products.

The Program Development Objective is to (i) reduce carbon emission and cost of operation for Thailand, (ii) improve air quality, and (iii) tap into the potential of the carbon market to offset the cost of investments with short-term and no regret interventions that are proposed to be implemented in the coming years to enable immediate actions of stakeholders to move towards a green and climate-resilient future. The program aims to support Thailand to reduce carbon emissions and move towards a green and climate resilient future through the following interventions: • Increasing renewable energy (RE) generation capacity for captive consumption • Improving energy efficiency (EE) in buildings • Upgrading to LED streetlights • Transition to electric vehicles

The proposed VPA aims to increase renewable energy generation capacity via solar photovoltaic (PV) installation in public and private buildings. Thailand has immense potential for solar-based projects. While large-scale solar farms require large land-use, rooftop solar can utilize the space on the rooftops of buildings or in and around as captive ground-mounted solar installations within the premises of the buildings in cities. Thus, installing solar for buildings is a practical measure to reduce emissions and energy demand for cities. The VPA entails the installation of rooftop and ground-mounted solar PV systems for captive (self-consumption) use in Thailand. The VPA will generate approximately 20,126 MWh annually and achieve 8,030 tCO2 in annual emission reductions.

KPC intends to develop a bamboo plantation designed to address socio-economic and environmental challenges in the Philippines. Bamboo is known for its high carbon sequestration capabilities. One of our goals is to contribute to greenhouse gas (GHG) removals thereby generating high integrity carbon credits representing verified greenhouse gas removals over the crediting period and also providing jobs and economic returns to the IP communities. The geographic region of the project is in Cotabato province in the Philippines within the two Municipalities of President Roxas and Arakan. The project will be implemented on IPs’ ancestral lands within the defined project boundary. The project will provide a sustainable and steady source of livelihood for IP communities that will help address rural poverty and will provide the new generation of IP’s better opportunities in life. It will foster rural development, strengthen food security, and promote social stability through sustainable employment generation. It will also foster collaboration between the private and public sectors to further develop the Philippine bamboo industry.

The US SecondCrop Project removes atmospheric CO₂ by applying CarbonBuilder, a patented fungal seed coating, to corn and soybean crops across US Midwest farmland. Root-associated fungi intercept plant-derived carbon and convert it into Mineral-Associated Organic Carbon (MAOC), physically bound to soil minerals and proven to persist for centuries. No land use change, new equipment, or altered crop rotations are required.

In Laos consistent access to safe, potable water remains a critical challenge, forcing many rural communities to rely on contaminated sources. To mitigate health risks, households traditionally boil water over biomass and charcoal fires—a practice that is labor intensive, environmentally taxing, and is a significant contributor to deforestation and indoor air pollution. TerraClear, a social enterprise based in Laos, addresses this issue through the manufacture and distribution of locally produced ceramic water filters. These gravity-fed household treatment systems require zero energy input, providing a sustainable, emissions-free alternative to traditional boiling. By replacing carbon-intensive water treatment with this clean technology, the project directly reduces greenhouse gas emissions and waterborne diseases while simultaneously improving school attendance and productivity. With the support of carbon finance, TerraClear will continue to scale its operations to reach hundreds of thousands of families and create sustainable jobs in rural areas, ensuring that clean water access no longer comes at the cost of vital forest resources.

Aksa Yenilenebilir Enerji Üretim A.Ş. plans to launch the Alıç Solar Power Plant Project with a total installed capacity of 50.00 MWp / 50.00 MWe, based on the Electricity Generation License obtained from the Energy Market Regulatory Authority on 04/12/2025. The project will be implemented within the borders Kamanlı District, Kırşehir Province, Türkiye. As part of the project, a solar power plant will be constructed, and a Battery Energy Storage System will also be established. The grid connection of the plant will be realized as an in-and-out connection to the Kızılırmak–Kırşehir transmission line at the 154 kV voltage level.

The Granadillos Wind Park project consists of the development of a 50 MW wind power facility located in Villa Vázquez, Montecristi province, aimed at supplying renewable electricity to the national grid. The project is expected to generate approximately 153 GWh annually using wind turbines. It will contribute to climate change mitigation (SDG 13) and support access to affordable and clean energy (SDG 7). Additionally, it will promote economic growth and job creation (SDG 8), generating up to 350 jobs during construction and around 15 permanent positions during operation and maintenance.

The Matafongo Solar Park project consists of the development of a 50 MWac photovoltaic facility located in Sabana Buey village, Peravia province, aimed at supplying renewable electricity to the national grid (SENI). The project is expected to generate approximately 118 GWh annually and reduce around 80,000 tCO₂e per year. It will contribute to climate change mitigation (SDG 13) and support access to affordable and clean energy (SDG 7). Additionally, it will promote economic growth and job creation (SDG 8), generating up to 350 jobs during construction and around 15 permanent positions during operation and maintenance.

The project aims to reduce deforestation in Tanzania by replacing inefficient traditional cookstoves with improved stoves that use renewable biomass as fuel, providing a cleaner alternative to firewood. The main goals are to cut carbon emissions from firewood use, improve community health and air quality, and generate local employment opportunities.

The primary objective of this project is to rehabilitate broken and non-functional boreholes to provide clean and safe drinking water to local communities in Malawi. This initiative addresses the need for alternative water purification methods, reducing the reliance on boiling water for drinking purposes and thereby improving the living conditions of the population. The project alleviates the burden on rural women and children, who often bear the responsibility of collecting water and firewood by ensuring access to clean drinking water within 1 kilometre of households. Consequently, this project reduces carbon dioxide emissions associated with the combustion process traditionally used for water purification. In addition to its environmental impact, the project significantly enhances the quality of life, health, and socio-economic status of beneficiaries in the water-stressed regions of Malawi. It includes hygiene awareness campaigns to improve sanitation among local inhabitants. Furthermore, it creates employment opportunities for young people through installing and maintaining rehabilitated boreholes.

The primary purpose of this project is to address the acute water crisis in Tanzania by providing sustainable access to safe drinking water for households, institutional buildings, and nearby communities through water stations. A key aspect of the project is the improvement of public health by reducing the incidence of waterborne diseases such as cholera, dysentery, and typhoid. Additionally, the project emphasizes community engagement and education, involving local communities in the maintenance and management of water systems and educating them on best practices for water use and hygiene. The project alleviates the burden of water collection on women and girls, freeing up time for education and economic activities. It will also reduce energy consumption by minimizing the need for boiling water with wood or charcoal, thereby lowering energy costs and deforestation. Furthermore, the project will promote decent work and economic growth by generating local jobs in the installation, maintenance, and distribution of water purification systems, fostering economic development.

Aksa Yenilenebilir Enerji Üretim A.Ş. plans to launch the Mersin Power Plant Project with Energy Storage a total installed capacity of 112.00 MWm/100.08 MWe, based on the Electricity Generation License obtained from the Energy Market Regulatory Authority on 20/03/2025. The project will be implemented within the borders of Üçoluk, Çukurasma, and Sütlüce neighborhoods in Gülnar District, Mersin Province, Türkiye. As part of the project, a wind power plant will be constructed, and a Battery Energy Storage System will also be established. The grid connection of the plant will be realized as a permanent connection to the 154 kV Akkuyu 380 Transformer Substation, and temporarily as a tap connection to the 154 kV Gezende–Taşucu transmission line. As it’s scheduled to be commissioned in October 2026, the Mersin WPP with Energy Storage is expected to supply approximately 400,320 MWh of electricity annually to the grid. Due to its renewable energy source, the wind power plant will also contribute to a reduction of approximately 249,880 tons of CO₂ equivalent emissions per year.

The purpose of the VPA is to disseminate Household Water Treatment (HWT) technologies in domestic households and Institutional Water Treatment technologies (IWT) in Early Childhood Development Centers (ECD) in the Republic of Rwanda, Africa. These HWT/IWTs are distributed to beneficiaries which were earlier using wood and/or charcoal on rudimentary stoves for boiling water or were consuming untreated water. The project makes the end-users energy efficient and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions otherwise resulting from the burning of non-renewable woody biomass and/or charcoal for boiling unsafe water to make it safe for consumption. The WPS distributed under this VPA are ceramic water filters and consume no electricity or fuel. The project boundary is the geographical boundary of Rwanda where these filters are distributed in phased implementation throughout the crediting period.

The EOS Climate – High-Integrity Climate & Social Impact Programme is a Programme of Activities (PoA) developed under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG) framework, aligned with the Paris Agreement. The Programme is coordinated and managed by EOS Climate as the Coordinating and Managing Entity (CME). The Programme addresses greenhouse gas emissions associated with the use of non-renewable biomass fuels for boiling and sterilizing water in rural and peri-urban communities across Malawi. In the baseline scenario, households rely on unsafe water sources and boil water using firewood or charcoal, resulting in adverse health impacts, time burdens on women and children, local deforestation, and significant GHG emissions. The Programme enables access to safe, reliable, and continuous drinking water through the installation of solar-powered artesian borehole systems with communal tap stands. All project activities operate with zero direct GHG emissions, eliminating the need for biomass combustion at the point of water use. The geographical boundary is national in scope, covering eligible rural and peri-urban areas across Malawi. Individual Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs) are developed and included under the PoA framework over time, in accordance with Gold Standard requirements.

The Wells of Life – Sustainable Safe Water for Malawi is a voluntary carbon mitigation Programme of Activities (PoA) registered under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG), coordinated and managed by EOS Climate and Energy Ltd as the Coordinating and Managing Entity (CME). The Programme is designed to improve continuous access to safe and reliable drinking water in underserved communities in Malawi, while reducing greenhouse gas emissions associated with the boiling of drinking water using non-renewable biomass fuels. VPA-1, the first real case Voluntary Project Activity under the PoA, covers 19 solar-powered groundwater well systems implemented across the Southern Region of Malawi, spanning the districts of Machinga, Zomba, Mulanje, Thyolo, and Blantyre. The Programme applies the Safe Drinking Water Supply (SDWS v2.0) methodology and contributes to SDG 3, 5, 6, 7, 13, and 15. No financial burden is placed on end-users; access to safe drinking water is provided free of charge to beneficiary communities.

The TDV Safe Water Supply Project, developed by Türkiye Diyanet Vakfı (TDV), aims to improve access to clean and safe drinking water through the construction and operation of deep community boreholes. The project includes drilling boreholes into protected underground aquifers, installing solar- or generator-powered pumping systems, elevated water storage tanks, and water distribution points. The project is expected to improve public health and living conditions by providing reliable access to hygienic water, reducing dependence on unsafe water sources, and decreasing the time spent collecting water.

The PoA "Water for People – Clean Water Access Programme in Africa" targets peri-urban and rural communities and institutions in Rwanda, Malawi, and Uganda, where many still rely on unsafe water sources and purify their water by boiling it over wood-fueled stoves. Across these three countries, existing water infrastructure is often inadequate or in disrepair due to limited maintenance capacity and insufficient water treatment. Under this PoA, Water For People, in collaboration with government authorities and community WASH committees, will install, rehabilitate, and maintain thousands of water points in each country to deliver reliable, safe water to communities and institutions. By providing safe drinking water without the need for fuel, the programme directly reduces greenhouse gas emissions while improving health and livelihoods.

The purpose of this project is to modernize paddy cultivation in Bangladesh by promoting and implementing the alternate wetting and drying (AWD) method in project farms/areas. The AWD method promoted under the project is designed to optimize water usage in paddy cultivation by alternating periods of wetting and drying. This technique reduces water consumption and improves soil aeration, as a result methane emissions from paddy fields are significantly reduced contributing to lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

The purpose of this project is to modernize paddy cultivation in Bangladesh by promoting and implementing the alternate wetting and drying (AWD) method in project farms/areas. The AWD method promoted under the project is designed to optimize water usage in paddy cultivation by alternating periods of wetting and drying. This technique reduces water consumption and improves soil aeration, as a result methane emissions from paddy fields are significantly reduced contributing to lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

The “SCETA - Supporting a Sustainable Circular Economy Transition in Agriculture for Carbon Neutralization” aims to generate carbon credits through the enhancement of soil carbon sequestration in Kazakhstan. Improved sequestration is achieved by introducing sustainable agricultural practices to local farmers. The project provides advisory services and access to sustainable agricultural best practices, as well as implementation of an improved monitoring system to measure achieved results against the baseline.

The Belize Coastal Sargassum Resilience and Circularity Project aims to intercept and process sargassum biomass and eligible biodegradable organic matter to avoid methane emissions from uncontrolled decomposition and landfill disposal. The project combines controlled aerobic treatment, decentralized organic waste processing, and circular resource recovery to transform intercepted biomass into beneficial products, including biochar-enriched compost for local use. Implemented initially in Caye Caulker, Belize, in collaboration with local stakeholders, the project is designed to strengthen coastal resilience, support sustainable land management, reduce environmental impacts associated with sargassum accumulation, and contribute to measurable climate mitigation outcomes under Gold Standard methodologies.

EA Energy Ltd. plans to implement the Abaco Solar Power Plant with Energy Storage Project on Abaco Island, The Bahamas. The project activity consists of a solar power plant integrated with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in order to enhance grid stability, improve renewable electricity integration, and support sustainable energy generation within the island. The project activity is expected to contribute significantly to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by supplying renewable electricity to the island grid system while reducing dependence on fossil fuel-based electricity generation. In addition, the Battery Energy Storage System will support the reliability and flexibility of the electricity network by enabling better management of intermittent renewable energy generation.

Amazi Water Carbon Credit Program in Burundi acts as a bridge between climate action and community development. This program allows communities to gain access to safe water through boreholes and solar-powered supply systems, leaving out the need to boil water using firewood or charcoal. This translates into measurable emission savings, which can be certified as carbon credits under the Gold Standard. Through this program, communities of Burundi enjoy uninterrupted access to safe water, which reduces waterborne diseases, improves public health, and protect forests by reducing demand for firewood, while cutting carbon emissions that contribute to climate change. The program provides a mechanism to sustain water infrastructure, improve health outcomes, protect the environment, and empower communities, all while contributing to global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

UpEnergy would ensure the last-mile distribution/installation of the energy efficient/clean energy technologies to the beneficiaries. This VPA is implemented in host country-Zambia.

The Amru Rice AWD Project in Cambodia supports the adoption of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) in irrigated rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions while maintaining stable yields and farmer livelihoods. The project replaces continuous flooding with controlled wetting and drying cycles, using water-level pipes to guide irrigation timing and ensure safe drainage thresholds. By reducing anaerobic soil conditions in paddy fields, AWD can significantly lower methane emissions while also improving irrigation water efficiency. The project is expected to scale to beyond 20,000 hectares. The project is being co-developed by Amru Rice Cambodia and CarbonFarm, with both parties acting as project proponents. Amru Rice Cambodia leads on-ground implementation, while CarbonFarm supports as a technical partner through digital MRV tools, including satellite imagery, AI-based field monitoring, and selected IoT devices to strengthen data traceability.

In partnership with Hanns R. Neumann Stiftung, GrowGrounds is transforming coffee monocultures in Brazil’s Mantiqueira region into regenerative agroforestry systems that sequester carbon, restore biodiversity, and strengthen farm resilience. Over a 30-year period, the initiative will convert 500 to 1,500 hectares of coffee land and engage more than 200 smallholder farmers. By integrating trees into coffee systems compatible with mechanized harvesting and cattle grazing, the project provides a scalable model that improves soil health, enhances climate resilience, and supports landscape restoration. Beyond carbon sequestration, the project generates strong social and environmental benefits. Farmers receive 70% of carbon revenues, benefit from improved working conditions through shade-grown systems, and gain diversified long-term income opportunities. The project area borders the Serra do Papagaio State Park, a protected area of approx. 22,917 hectares within the Mantiqueira Mountain Range, a critical water source for southeastern Brazil. The park conserves remnants of the Atlantic Forest biome, one of the world’s most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems. To assess biodiversity impacts and guide monitoring, the project applies the IUCN's RHINO framework, with a focus on key species including the Maldonado Redbelly Toad, Buffy-tufted-ear marmoset, Ochre-breasted Pipit, Vinaceous-breasted Amazon, Sickle-winged Nightjar, and Luderwaldt's Highland Frog.

The Regular VPA Future Radici, Casoni represents a pivotal and strategic initiative within the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) Future Radici. Located in the municipality of Cassano allo Ionio (Cosenza), the project spans a total area of 129.59 hectars. These lands are owned by Leone Alato SpA. The project envisions the planting of approximately 122,500 trees, with the goal of transforming these agricultural lands into thriving, biodiverse forest ecosystems. The primary objective is to establish native and ecologically rich forest environments through a combination of afforestation and agroforestry practices. These practices are carefully tailored to the pedoclimatic and ecological characteristics of each site, ensuring that the interventions enhance biodiversity, support complex habitats, and maximize long-term carbon sequestration. The forest models adopted in this project are non-extractive, the harvesting of timber or biomass is explicitly excluded. This commitment extends for a minimum duration of 60 years. To quantify the carbon absorption, the project will rely on methodologies recommended by the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). These methods will be calibrated using national and regional data. The goal is to produce credits that are measurable, verifiable, and directly linked to positive outcomes in both biodiversity and social impact.

The project enables rice growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh to transition from conventional continuously flooded rice cultivation to Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD). The core purpose is to reduce methane emissions from paddy fields while improving water efficiency, strengthening climate resilience, and increasing farmer livelihoods through a single scalable intervention. In the first instance the project is implemented in the Srikakulam and vizinagaram villages of Andhra Pradesh in 5,041 ha of land which reduces 6,710 tCO2e/year. Detail climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions Mitigation: The project delivers climate mitigation benefits by reducing methane generation in paddy fields. AWD shortens the duration of continuous flooding, allowing aerobic soil conditions to form, which: Significantly reduces methane emissions, the dominant emission source in irrigated paddy Lowers energy-related emissions due to reduced irrigation pumping demand Prevents soil carbon loss caused by over-flooding and anaerobic conditions The transition is expected to generate substantial emission reductions across all participating fields under the project boundary. Adaptation: AWD strengthens climate resilience in farming systems and communities by: Reducing water consumption, helping farmers cope with erratic rainfall and declining groundwater Improving soil aeration and root development, enabling crops to better tolerate climatic stress Lowering irrigation costs and farm expenses, increasing financial resilience Improving access to technical support and knowledge through farmer training and field demonstrations By promoting a climate-responsive irrigation practice, the project supports long-term adaptation to rising temperatures and water scarcity in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh of Indian states.

The project supports smallholder farmers in integrating agroforestry practices into existing agricultural lands to improve livelihoods, strengthen ecosystem resilience, and promote sustainable land management. The project involves planting and maintaining a mix of native fruit and timber tree species within farming systems. Fruit trees provide regular income and food security benefits, while timber species offer long-term economic value. These interventions also improve soil health, reduce soil erosion, enhance soil moisture retention, and increase vegetation cover. The project contributes to climate change mitigation through carbon sequestration in tree biomass and enhancement of soil organic carbon, generating measurable and verifiable greenhouse gas removals under the Gold Standard Land Use and Forests (LUF) framework. By diversifying farm income and restoring degraded landscapes, the project aims to deliver long-term climate, environmental, and socio-economic benefits for participating rural communities.

Net Zero Ag Limited plans a Programme of Activities that aims to reduce methane emissions associated with conventional farming (CF) techniques. The first small-scale project activities will start in Narowal and Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan on May 2026. Rice cultivation is one of the main GHG sources within the agriculture sector and generates approximately 8.5 MtCO2e of methane per year — roughly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Conventional flooding-based production practices generate significant methane emissions and consume large volumes of fresh water. The programme will introduce the technique of alternate wetting and drying (AWD) to rice farmers in Pakistan. By adaptation of the technique, controlled irrigation strategy implemented will significantly reduce methane emissions, water use, and pumping costs.

The Parmakören Solar BESS Project is a newly built grid-connected solar photovoltaic power plant integrated with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), located in Kütahya, Türkiye. The project owner is Ecowind 1 Enerji A.Ş. The project has a total installed capacity of 60.4 MWp (50 MWe), with a predicted annual electricity supply to the grid of 100,000 MWh.

This VPA deploys efficient improved cookstoves (ICS), reducing woody biomass consumption for Urban and peri-urban households in the Republic of Malawi. The scenario existing prior to the implementation of the project is the use of very inefficient traditional cookstoves or 3- stone fires, consuming a lot of non-renewable charcoal and firewood. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils’ reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer.

The primary objective of the Programme of Activities (PoA) is to establish and manage 10,000 ha of agroforestry plantations on croplands across the states of Gujarat and Rajasthan through the implementation of multiple Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs). The PoA aims to promote sustainable land-use practices by introduction of diverse tree species. Through active engagement with local farmers and stakeholders, the PoA initiative will not only sequester approximately 2,433,999 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period but also plays a crucial role in developing resilient agroforestry systems that not only restore ecological balance but also deliver long-term social and economic benefits to local farmer communities. The first real case VPA under this PoA, implemented a small scale agroforestry plantation of 98 ha which sequesters 10,889 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period across multiple districts of Gujarat, India, which involves the plantation of multiple agroforestry species on agricultural land. By actively engaging local farmers, the VPA seeks to create resilient agroforestry plantations that generate long term ecological, economic and social benefits for the community.

The project aims to provide households and institutions in Bhutan with electric cooking and space-heating technologies to reduce GHG emissions from the use of firewood, biomass, and fossil fuels. Developed under GS, the project will deliver verified emission reductions and socio-economic benefits. For cooking, the project targets low-income households, schools, monasteries, fodder preparation, and small commercial establishments, including rural and high-altitude communities. In the absence of the project, cooking needs are primarily met through firewood, traditional stoves, and LPG, resulting in emissions, pressure on forest resources, and indoor air pollution. The project promotes efficient electric cooking technologies, including induction and infrared cookstoves powered by grid electricity. This transition reduces fuel consumption and emissions while improving indoor air quality, reducing cooking time and costs, and enhancing health and well-being. For space heating, the programme promotes the replacement of traditional biomass-based heating systems with efficient electric heaters, particularly in colder regions where firewood is the primary heating fuel. The intervention reduces fuel use, emissions, and pressure on forests while improving thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and living conditions. It also reduces the time and costs associated with fuel collection and purchase, especially benefiting women and supporting Bhutan’s low-carbon development objectives.

The project shall consist of the installation and operation of containerized biogas plants in the Philippines. The facilities will convert the organic waste to biogas. The biogas generated during the digestion of the organic waste will be subsequently utilized for the generation of renewable electricity. The digestate will be processed into fertilizer.

The project shall consist of the construction and operation of a biogas facility in the City of Naga on the island of Cebu, Philippines. The facility will convert the organic fraction of municipal solid waste to biogas. The biogas generated during the digestion of the organic waste will be subsequently utilized for the generation of renewable energy.

The project will produce and distribute char-briquettes made from agricultural residues, primarily coconut shells, as a sustainable cooking fuel for households and street food vendors in Cambodia. Agricultural residues are crushed, carbonized in a rotary carbonization furnace, mixed with a binder, and pressed into uniform briquettes under high pressure. The project uses waste heat recovered from the pyrolysis process for drying, improving energy efficiency and ensuring low residual moisture and consistent product quality. The briquettes are intended to replace traditional wood charcoal, thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions and pressure on forest resources.

+SOL, the Mozambique Accelerator for Off-grid Electrification, is a programme supporting the expansion of affordable clean energy access in rural and underserved areas through private-sector deployment of solar green mini-grids, solar home systems and related clean energy solutions, in line with Mozambique’s national electrification priorities. The programme also includes a Climate Asset Aggregator function to integrate carbon finance into the off-grid electrification model, including the development and registration of eligible clean energy activities under the Gold Standard framework. Through this structure, emission reductions generated by supported assets can be quantified, certified and monetised to help strengthen the financial sustainability and scale-up of off-grid electrification in Mozambique.

The Integra Solar Park I project consists of a 13.7 MWp (9.9 MWac) grid-connected photovoltaic power plant located in San Antonio de Guerra, Santo Domingo Province, Dominican Republic. The project will generate approximately 22,809 MWh of renewable electricity annually, supplying clean energy to the national grid (SENI) and reducing around 14,825 tCO₂e per year. By increasing the share of renewable energy in the country’s electricity mix, the project contributes to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) through the creation of employment opportunities during construction and operation.

The Integra Solar Park II project consists of a 8.5 MWp (7.3 MWn) grid-connected photovoltaic power plant located in San Antonio de Guerra, Santo Domingo Province, Dominican Republic. The project will generate approximately 14,544 MWh of renewable electricity annually, supplying clean energy to the national grid (SENI) and reducing around 9,454 tCO₂e per year. By increasing the share of renewable energy in the country’s electricity mix, the project contributes to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) through the creation of employment opportunities during construction and operation.

The SAG Solar Park project consists of a 25.7 MWp (19.8 MWn-ac) grid-connected photovoltaic power plant located in San Antonio de Guerra, Santo Domingo Province, Dominican Republic. By increasing the share of renewable energy in the country’s electricity mix, the project contributes to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) through the creation of employment opportunities during construction and operation.

The project proponent is Rossmann Beteiligungs GmbH. The project “Rossmann Nicaragua - Reforesting diverse native tree species in East Nicaragua” is an ambitious private-led environmental project aimed at transforming 936 hectares of degraded slash & burn land in the tropical lowland of East Nicaragua into a thriving, diverse native forest ecosystem. The project activities encompass an afforestation/reforestation activity that mitigates climate change: The establishment of a mainly native tree species reforestation at an area which has been used so far for cattle, applying „slash and burn“ practices for at least the last two decades. The cattle was grazing throughout the majority of the year and the bush was burned down and slashed frequently to enable new grass growth. The project does not only include the reforestation of 21 mainly native trees but also additional forest islands, 200 ha which were protected from slash & burn and are not eligible as project activities. They serve as biodiversity habitats and bridges for wandering animals seeking new habitats. The local communities in the neighborhoods will be involved in the project as additional jobs and benefits will be created. The project site will be operated by Ritter Sport Nicaragua, who represents an adjacent certified Gold Standard afforestation project.

The Data-Verified Smart Induction Stove Project in Rwanda is a large-scale clean cooking project that promotes the adoption of modern electric cooking technologies by replacing traditional charcoal and firewood stoves with IoT-enabled smart induction stoves. The project will distribute up to 100,000 induction stoves to grid-connected households across urban and peri-urban areas of Rwanda, enabling a transition to cleaner, more efficient, and sustainable cooking practices. The project applies the Gold Standard Metered & Measured Energy Cooking Devices Methodology V2.0 and utilizes ATEC's proprietary digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) platform to continuously record electricity consumption and stove usage. This real-time monitoring ensures accurate, transparent, and fully auditable quantification of greenhouse gas emission reductions. By displacing the use of non-renewable biomass fuels, the project reduces greenhouse gas emissions, lowers household cooking costs and improves indoor air quality. It also creates local employment opportunities and supports sustained adoption of clean cooking through user engagement and performance-based incentives. The project contributes to Rwanda's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and several Sustainable Development Goals, including Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), Climate Action (SDG 13), Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 8), and No Poverty (SDG 1).

Agriculture is one of the most important sectors of the Egyptian economy. In many areas, precipitation levels are low, meaning that agricultural activity can only be sustained through irrigation. This POA aims to provide the rural farmers in Egypt by supporting the transition to solar PV systems to power irrigation systems. The solar PV systems will help to displace inefficient irrigation systems that are powered by diesel generators. The solar-based solutions can provide reliable, cost effective and environmentally sustainable energy source for the decentralised and informal sectors. When deployed, the benefits include improved livelihoods (increased productivity and incomes, and food security), increased social welfare (poverty alleviation, emissions reduction) and reduced spending on fossil fuel subsidies and centralized infrastructure.
